html: The same standard names the main families of robots. An industrial robot (clause 3.6) is an “automatically controlled, reprogrammable multipurpose manipulator, programmable in three or more axes, which can be either fixed in place or fixed to a mobile platform for use in automation applications in an industrial environment” (clause cross-references left out). A service robot (3.7) is a “robot in personal use or professional use that performs useful tasks for humans or equipment.” A medical robot (3.8) is one “intended to be used as medical electrical equipment or medical electrical systems,” and ISO says it is counted as neither an industrial nor a service robot.[3] The International Federation of Robotics (IFR), which publishes the world’s robot statistics, still counts medical robots among service robots, so the two sources split the categories slightly differently.[4][5] Finally, robotics itself (3.10) is the “science and practice of designing, manufacturing, and applying robots.”[3]

The welding arm from section 01 passes every test in clause 3.6: it is automatically controlled, it can be reprogrammed for a new car model, it has six axes and it works in a factory. The IFR says it uses the ISO 8373 definitions when it counts robots for its World Robotics reports.[6][7]

ISO is not the only voice. Older textbooks often quote the Robot Institute of America (RIA), which in 1979 described a robot as “a reprogrammable, multifunctional manipulator designed to move material, parts, tools, or specialized devices” through programmed motions to do a variety of tasks.[10] Researchers who study mobile and intelligent robots tend to define robots by what they do. George Bekey of the University of Southern California writes, “We frequently define a robot as a machine that senses, thinks, and acts.”[11] He also stresses that a robot “is a physical system situated in the real world, and is not only software residing on a computer,” and that it is not a living organism.[12] IEEE Spectrum’s ROBOTS guide gives a similar version: “A robot is an autonomous machine capable of sensing its environment, carrying out computations to make decisions, and performing actions in the real world.”[13]

Autonomy is the part of the ISO definition that separates a robot from an ordinary machine. ISO 8373 defines it as the “ability to perform intended tasks based on current state and sensing, without human intervention.” A note adds that, for a given application, the degree of autonomy can be judged by “the quality of decision-making” and the “independence from human.”[3] In other words, autonomy is not yes or no. A machine can have a little or a lot.

What about a machine with no autonomy at all, such as an arm that a person drives with a joystick? ISO gives it a separate name: a robotic device, a “mechanism developed with robotic technology, but not fulfilling all characteristics of a robot.” Its examples are a “Teleoperated remote manipulator, haptic device, end-effector, unpowered exoskeleton”—where a haptic device is a force-feedback interface and an end-effector is the robot’s tool or gripper.[3] ISO 8373 itself lists a teleoperated (remotely operated) manipulator as an example of a robotic device rather than a robot.[14] Real robots often mix the two modes. ISO notes that a mobile robot (“robot able to travel under its own control”) can also have a way to be remotely controlled, and the IEEE guide says many robots combine remote control with operation that needs no human.[3][13]

SAE assigns a level to the driving feature that is switched on at a given moment, not to the car as a whole, and it leaves out momentary interventions such as automatic emergency braking.[16] That is a useful habit for robots too: ask how autonomous a machine is while doing a particular task.

Drone: the IEEE guide lists drones among robots that “take to the skies.”[13] Under ISO, a drone flown entirely by a pilot looks more like a robotic device, while one that holds its position or flies a route by itself has the autonomy to be a mobile robot.

One more distinction is worth keeping. Every robot is a kind of automation, but not every piece of automation is a robot. A fixed conveyor belt or a machine built for a single job is automated but is not reprogrammable or multipurpose, which are the words ISO uses to mark the line.

Hybrid (three-layer). Many robots combine the two. Erann Gat described a common pattern with three layers: a controller that runs fast feedback loops between sensors and actuators, a sequencer that chooses which behavior to run, and a deliberator that does slow planning and search.[27][28] Gat’s reasoning was that pure planning is too slow for a changing world, while pure reaction trusts sensors that are often unreliable.[28]

In 1961 the first Unimate went to work at General Motors, at GM’s plant in Ewing Township near Trenton, New Jersey. The plant was then run by the Ternstedt division of GM’s Fisher Body unit (it was later called Inland Fisher Guide), which is why sources call it the Ternstedt plant.[17][23][24] The job was handling hot die-cast parts. The arm, about 4,000 lb (1,800 kg), lifted die-cast pieces of up to about 40 lb and dropped them into cooling pools, a hot and dangerous job that three shifts of workers had done before.[23] After roughly 100,000 hours of work the robot was donated to the Smithsonian in 1971, and the Unimate joined the Robot Hall of Fame in 2003.[23][20]

2008, the UR5: in December 2008 Universal Robots, founded in 2005 in Odense, Denmark, sold its UR5 to Linatex, a Danish maker of technical plastics and rubber, to tend a CNC machine. It is generally described as the first commercially viable collaborative robot, and it needed no safety cage. By December 2018 the company had sold more than 27,000 cobots.[31][17]

The ABB IRB 360 FlexPicker is a well-known delta. Depending on the version it has 3 or 4 axes, payloads of 1 to 8 kg, and a working diameter of 1130 or 1600 mm. Its position repeatability is 0.1 mm. On ABB’s standard 25/305/25 mm pick path, the lightest version manages a cycle time as low as 0.30 s, although ABB notes that cycle times “may vary depending on the actual application.”[12]

Collaborative robots, or cobots, are designed to work alongside people in shared spaces. Their speed and force limits are configured as part of their setup, and many can be taught by lead-through, a form of hand guiding: the operator physically guides the arm through the waypoints of a task.[14] Universal Robots’ e-Series, programmed through PolyScope 5, is a common example.[15]

The safety standard for industrial robots changed in March 2025, when ISO 10218-1:2025 and ISO 10218-2:2025 replaced the 2011 versions. The revised standard no longer uses the terms “collaborative robot” or “collaborative operation.” It speaks of a collaborative application instead, because only the actual application can be confirmed as collaborative.[16] The revision also folds in the old cobot guidance, ISO/TS 15066, including limits on the forces and pressures allowed if a robot touches a person, and it splits robots into two classes.[16][17]

MiR1200 Pallet Jack (2024): fuses four depth cameras and a 3D lidar to spot obstacles on the floor and overhead, reroutes itself, and uses AI pallet detection trained on over 1.2 million real and synthetic images. It is designed to comply with ISO 3691-4.[25]

Safety standards: mobile robots have their own standards, separate from ISO 10218. In the United States, ANSI/RIA R15.08-1 (2020) sets safety requirements for manufacturers of industrial mobile robots, and ANSI/A3 R15.08-2 (October 2023) covers integrators, including fleets, charging stations and the surrounding environment. A Part 3 for users was still to come at the time.[26] Internationally, ISO 3691-4 covers driverless industrial trucks and their systems; its current edition is from 2023, and a third edition was in draft in 2026.[27]

OSHA lists the sources of these hazards as human programming errors, control errors, unauthorized access, mechanical failure, time pressure and power system failures.[2] Each case above maps to a habit you can build from day one: know the program, use the enabling device, lock out before servicing, and never enter the cell in automatic mode.

OSHA also says that anyone who programs, operates or maintains a robot should receive adequate safety training before being assigned, and that removing or engineering away a hazard is preferred over relying on rules and protective equipment.[2] The main international standard is ISO 10218, revised in 2025. The new edition makes functional safety requirements more explicit, absorbs the cobot guidance from ISO/TS 15066, and adds cybersecurity requirements as they relate to safety.[3] Its collaborative modes were introduced in 1.3 Types of Robots.

For industrial roles, vendor training counts. FANUC America, for example, runs its own training courses with recommended paths in programming, vision, safety and more.[27] One example entry course, FANUC HandlingTool Operation and Programming at Kent State, runs 32 hours with 24 lab exercises, has no prerequisites, and leads to the FANUC Robotics CERT I credential.[7] Universal Robots Academy offers free e-learning for its e-Series robots, including an 8-module Core Track that simulates setting up and programming a complete pick-and-place application.[28] The Association for Advancing Automation (A3) also certifies robot integrator companies, and offers individual credentials such as Certified Motion Control Professional.[29]

Robots that work around people need predictable behavior. A hospitality robot in a hotel is often organized as a state machine (a model where a robot switches between distinct operational states based on inputs), such as Idle (waiting for a wake word), Listening and Responding, with a rule that the robot slows or stops whenever a person comes too close.

Nuclear and hazardous sites: after the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi accident, iRobot PackBots entered the reactor buildings on April 17–18, 2011[31][32] to measure radiation and record video, and the Japanese robot Quince followed in July 2011 (section 11).[33]

The RAPID example in 2.3 Common Programming Languages uses all of these ideas. pHome is a robtarget, a Cartesian position and orientation. MoveJ pHome, v1000, z50, tGripper is a joint move that blends within 50 mm, and MoveL ... fine, tGripper is a straight-line move that stops exactly. Both use tGripper, the gripper tool defined in that example, so the TCP is at the gripper, 150 mm out from the mounting flange, rather than at the bare flange. No work object is given, so the targets are measured in wobj0, the base frame.[17][25]

In the last lesson we looked at the arm itself. An arm bolted to the floor with nothing around it cannot do useful work: it has no part to pick up, no tool, no way of knowing when the next part has arrived, and nothing to protect a person who walks too close. To make it productive, engineers build a robot cell around it.

The International Federation of Robotics (IFR) uses the ISO 8373:2021 definition of an industrial robot: an “automatically controlled, reprogrammable, multipurpose manipulator, programmable in three or more axes,” which can be fixed in place or mobile and is used in industrial automation.[1] That definition covers the machine you buy from a robot maker. The U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) widens the view. Its Technical Manual describes an industrial robot system as more than the robot itself. The system also includes the end-effector attached to the manipulator, the control system (its computers, processors and programs), power sources, sensors, and input/output interfaces. OSHA names four major components of the robot: the manipulator, the control system, the teach pendant and the end-effector. Adding the end-effector is what makes it an industrial robot system.[2]

A cell goes one step further: it is the robot system plus everything an integrator adds so that it can do one job safely and repeatably, from part feeding and sensors to a coordinating controller and guarding.
5. Part presentation: the hardware that brings parts to the robot in a known position and takes them away, such as infeed and outfeed conveyors, fixtures, nests, bowl feeders and pallet stations.

The teach pendant deserves a closer look because it is how people work near the robot. Its enabling device is “a manually operated control device which, when continuously activated and used in conjunction with a separate actuating (start) control, will allow the machine to function in manual operating mode.”[8] In other words, holding the enabling switch allows motion but does not start anything; a separate start or jog command is still needed.[8] Most enabling switches have three positions. If the operator does not hold the switch in its middle (set) position, the manipulator cannot move.[9]

Robot makers build these requirements into their products. Universal Robots' manuals, citing ISO 10218-2, state that some of its larger models (the UR15, UR20, UR30, UR8 Long and UR18) need an external enabling device or a three-position-enabling (3PE) teach pendant whenever someone programs or teaches within reach of the robot application.[10] Mode keys are not a substitute for lockout. In one fatal case investigated in Michigan, the gate key was meant to put the robot in manual mode before anyone entered, but the key system did not work properly and the gate had no interlock. A foreman entered without locking out the robot, which was still in automatic mode, and was pinned when the arm moved.[11]

The safeguards are what separate a robot cell from a robot on a bench. As summarized from the OSHA Technical Manual, the options include mechanical limiting devices, nonmechanical limiting devices, presence-sensing safeguarding devices, fixed barriers and interlocked barrier guards.[2][12] During automatic operation all safeguards should be active, and no part of the operator's body should be inside the safeguarded area.[12] An OSHA interpretation letter lists acceptable controls as “fixed barriers that are not easily defeated, barrier guards with interlocks that immediately stop machine motion, or presence-sensing devices that immediately stop machine motion,” and points to the ANSI/RIA R15.06-1999 robot safety standard.[13]

For a curtain fine enough to detect a finger or hand, K = 2000 mm/s and C = 8 × (d − 14 mm). If S comes out above 500 mm, the calculation is repeated with K = 1600 mm/s.[14][15] In a worked example from Keyence, T = 0.1157 s and C = 88 mm give S = 2000 × 0.1157 + 88 ≈ 319 mm.[14] (C = 88 mm corresponds to a 25 mm resolution, since 8 × (25 − 14) = 88.) The vendor guides do not agree on the minimum distances that apply when S is small, so a real installation must be checked against ISO 13855 itself.[14][15] A slow-stopping robot needs its light curtain farther away; a faster stop allows a more compact cell.

In the most common architecture the cell PLC is in charge. In PROFINET terms, a Siemens PLC acts as the IO-Controller and an ABB IRC5 robot controller acts as an IO-Device. PROFINET does not use the older PROFIBUS words “master” and “slave,”[16] although many engineers still say them: one forum post asks for a “Siemens PLC as master and IRC5 as slave” example project.[17] Status and command bits are exchanged cyclically, and one tutorial suggests a 1 ms update time as a starting point.[16] In smaller single-robot cells, such as a cobot tending one machine, the robot controller often runs the logic itself and reads simple inputs from the gripper, sensors and machine directly.

Because the robot and the PLC run separate programs, they coordinate through handshake signals. Control.com explains that handshakes are needed because external devices such as robots and CNC machines “do not have direct access to the internal programs of the control system or PLC.”[18] A simple handshake for one job looks like this (the signal names are examples):

Each side waits for the other's answer, so neither runs ahead if a signal is lost. The safety interlocks travel separately. Signals such as “E-stop OK” and “guard door closed” are either hard-wired from a safety PLC or safety relays, or sent over a safety protocol such as CIP Safety or PROFIsafe (safety-rated industrial network extensions designed to guarantee fail-safe communication over fieldbuses).[18] A safety protocol can share the same cable as ordinary data, but it is a separately rated path. Never make a person's safety depend on a normal handshake bit.

How does a factory know an integrator is competent? In North America, the Association for Advancing Automation (A3) runs a voluntary Certified Robot Integrator program. Integrators must already show “a high level of proficiency, experience and success” to be considered, and certification involves “an on-site audit, practical assessment of key personnel, safety training, and other important criteria.”[23] Certification lasts two years before it must be renewed.[23] The process includes pre-qualification, the on-site audit, a robot safety risk assessment and an exam.[24] The U.S. O*NET occupational database lists it as a credential that requires an exam and more than two years of experience.[25]

A cell project follows a fairly standard path, although each integrator names and splits the steps a little differently. It generally runs: application study with real part samples and a cycle-time estimate; concept layout and quote; detailed mechanical, tooling, electrical and controls design; risk assessment; simulation and offline programming; build and debug at the integrator's shop; the formal acceptance tests described below; and finally training, documentation and support.

The robot is rarely the slow part here. Cycle time in machine tending is driven by machining time, the door and chuck sequence, and reliable part presentation, not by the robot's top speed.[31] On an older machine, the robot can open and close the CNC door itself instead of the cell fitting an automatic door driven by a signal; Robotiq reports this works well in many integrations, while for a new machine an automatic door is generally worth its cost.[32]

A palletizing cell stacks cases onto pallets at the end of a packaging line. Pearson's RPC cell is a typical example: an empty pallet is dispensed onto a three-strand drag chain conveyor and carried to the loading position, and the robot places slip sheets (protective separator sheets that keep the stacked load stable) between layers when needed. Pearson rates it at 20 cases per minute steady state, with surges to 30.[33] Arpac's LT palletizer uses a “smart” infeed conveyor that separates the products, has a fully interlocked operator door and a light curtain, and is rated at up to 15 cases per minute.[34] Grippers are often vacuum plates.[35] The Arpac LT, for example, uses a dual-zone vacuum plate gripper that handles one or two cases at a time, and a light curtain guards the opening where full pallets leave the cell.[36] These are vendor ratings, not guarantees.

In a welding cell the operator's loading time can hide inside the robot's welding time. ABB's twin-station positioner (IRBP R) lets the robot weld on one side while the operator unloads and loads the other, with a screen between the two sides to block the arc light.[37] When both jobs are done, the positioner swaps the sides. Yaskawa states that the 250 kg version of its ArcWorld IV-6200SL positioner indexes between stations in 1.6 s and the 750 kg version in 2.2 s.[38] An earlier announcement gave 1.75 s and 2.5 s, so check the current datasheet before using a figure.[39]

About a quarter: a 2010 editorial in the journal Industrial Robot said that “various studies have concluded that an industrial robot represents around 25 percent of the total cost of implementation,” without naming the studies.[40]

Four to six times the robot: a Yaskawa Motoman director, quoted by Engineering.com, gave as a rule of thumb that integration “including safety, tooling, and programming will cost about four to six times the cost of the robot.”[41]

Label a cell layout. On paper or in a drawing tool, sketch a top view of a machine-tending cell about 4 m by 4 m and place and label these components: robot arm on a base; robot controller cabinet (outside the fence); teach pendant; gripper (EOAT) on the robot; CNC machine with its door facing the robot; infeed drawer for raw blanks; outfeed tray for finished parts; part-present sensor on the infeed; vision camera above the infeed; inspection gauge station; cell PLC and HMI panel (outside the fence); network switch; safety controller; perimeter fence; interlocked access gate; light curtain across the operator's loading opening; three emergency stop buttons. Then draw two kinds of lines: solid lines for data (PLC to robot, PLC to CNC, PLC to HMI) and dashed lines for safety signals (gate, light curtain and E-stops to the safety controller, safety controller to robot and CNC).

Trace one part through your cell. Write a numbered list of each step a single blank goes through, from the infeed drawer to the outfeed tray. For each step, name the device that acts and the signal that proves the step is complete. A starting point: (1) operator loads the drawer outside the light curtain; (2) the part-present sensor turns on; (3) the camera locates the blank; (4) the robot picks it with one side of a double gripper; (5) the robot waits for the CNC to report cycle done, spindle stopped and door confirmed open; (6) the robot unloads the finished part and loads the blank; (7) the robot leaves, reports clear, and the CNC closes its door and starts; (8) the robot places the finished part on the gauge, then on the outfeed tray. Mark which steps happen at the same time as machining.

In this capstone you build a complete robot work cell in software. A simulated arm picks a part from an infeed position, places it at an outfeed position, uses simulated I/O for its gripper and a part-present sensor, respects a safety configuration you set up yourself, and passes a test sheet modelled on a factory acceptance test (FAT: a formal check at the supplier's facility that the equipment meets the contract specifications before delivery). You can use either Universal Robots' URSim or ABB RobotStudio. Both are free to start, and both run the same controller software a real robot runs.

Following teaching-center guidance on project work, the grading criteria and the rubric are published now, at the start, rather than at the end. The work is split into milestones (a plan, a first working piece, an integrated demo, test evidence and a report), so that problems show up early while there is still time to fix them.[1] The final grade uses a four-level analytic rubric with no neutral middle level. An engineering-technology capstone program used the same format, rating each project from “Not Acceptable” to “Exemplary”.[2] The rubric is kept short on purpose: research on capstone rubrics notes that they must balance depth against simplicity, and that very detailed rubrics can narrow student creativity.[3] If you work in a team, you also hand in a short contribution statement at each milestone, because milestone evaluations are one documented way to keep each team member accountable to the group.[4][1]

Why a cell and not just a robot? A real cell also has fixtures, sensors, a gripper, guarding and a safety design (see 1.7). Building all of it teaches you to think like an integrator: what must be true before the robot moves, what happens when something fails, and how you prove the cell works.

In PolyScope, power on and release the brakes, set the TCP and payload for your gripper (see 2.5), define a feature frame for the infeed fixture, and teach Home, the pick and place points and their approach points as in 2.6. Save the installation and the program into the mounted folder, then stop and restart the container once to prove they survive.

The I/O is what makes this a cell rather than a motion demo. Before each pick, the program must wait for the part-present input. At the pick point it sets the gripper output and waits, either for a grip-confirmed input or for a fixed time. At the place point it clears the output and waits again. In the simulator nobody is going to put a real part on the infeed, so you toggle the part-present input yourself from the I/O screen (PolyScope) or the I/O simulator window (RobotStudio). That is also how you will test the cell in M4.

Add at least one error path. For example, if the grip is not confirmed within a time limit, open the gripper, retract to the approach point, and stop with a clear message instead of carrying an empty gripper to the place point. Lesson 2.7 shows the patterns for both RAPID and URScript.

Path A: PolyScope safety settings. PolyScope 5 has a dedicated safety menu that covers everything “from creating safety planes to limiting a joint's range of motion”; the current PolyScope 5 release is 5.24.[11] The PolyScope X handbook has matching sections on joint limits, safety planes and tool position restriction,[12] and its joint-limits page covers joint positions and speeds and notes that a wrist clamping-position protection is enabled by default.[13] The PolyScope 5 manuals cover setting a software safety password, the configurable safety functions and the software safety configuration.[14][15] From software 5.17, the System settings screens can be protected by the Admin password, and on new robots they are locked by default.[16] The exact menu steps were not checked for this course, so follow the handbook for your PolyScope version. Record what you observe rather than what you expect. Whether URSim's safety menu behaves exactly like a real controller, for example whether a plane violation triggers the same protective stop, was not confirmed by any source used for this course. If the robot does not react the way you expected, that is a valid and interesting result for your report.

Path B: ABB and SafeMove. ABB's safety option is SafeMove, but a participant on ABB's forum replied, while saying he was not sure, that “SafeMove runs on separate hardware which isn't simulated by the virtual controller”.[17] Forum users describe partial workarounds, such as starting the virtual controller separately to reach the Authenticate menu, or forcing safety I/O signals such as AS1 and AS2 (the dual automatic stop safety input channels monitored by ABB safety controllers) on so the robot can run.[17][18] These are community reports, not official procedures. The official reference is ABB's manual “Functional safety and SafeMove for OmniCore” (3HAC066559), which covers the system parameters, safety user grants and how to start Visual SafeMove.[19] For this project, use a programmed stand-in agreed with your instructor, such as a RAPID world zone or software axis limits, and say clearly in your report that it is a stand-in and not a safety function.

Sim settings do not carry over to a real cell. A safety configuration in a simulator is not a validated safety function. Speeds that look slow on screen, distances that look comfortable, and planes that stop a virtual robot say nothing about stopping distances, sensor placement or the performance level a real cell needs. A real cell needs a risk assessment and a validated safety design, as described in 5.4. Treat your M3 work as practice with the tools, not as a design you could install.

A factory acceptance test is a check, attended by the customer at the supplier before shipment, that confirms the equipment matches the contract specification, operates correctly and has its required safety functions.[20] Industry guidance lists safety items to check such as guarding and pinch points, sharp edges, whether limit switches and E-stops work and are well placed, and the built-in safety components.[21] FAT checklist templates are usually split into a documentation review, pre-test preparation and inspection steps, with items such as testing alarms, interlocks and emergency stops and checking that calibration and material certificates are available.[22]

Your simulated cell cannot have its guarding inspected, but it can be tested the same way. Every row of your test sheet needs an ID, the requirement it checks, the procedure, the expected result, the actual result, pass or fail, and the file name of the evidence (a screenshot or a log). Keep the limits of simulation in mind when you write up T04 to T06. A cell can pass a demonstration in the shop and still fail on site, because parameters, networks and interfaces differ there; integrators therefore treat the robot, controls, safety functions and plant interfaces as one system with documented acceptance criteria.[23] Your test sheet is a first version of those criteria, not a substitute for a real FAT and site acceptance test.

In this capstone you will program a simulated Universal Robots arm to pick up an object from a table and put it down somewhere else, using ROS 2 and MoveIt 2. The arm never touches real hardware. It runs on ros2_control mock hardware, and if you want physics you can move it into Gazebo. The planning is done with the MoveIt Task Constructor (MTC), which breaks a pick-and-place job into a chain of small, inspectable steps called stages.

You do not start from a blank page. The official MoveIt 2 tutorial "Pick and Place with MoveIt Task Constructor" is a complete, staged pipeline: it reads the current state, opens the hand, approaches, generates grasp poses and solves inverse kinematics for them, allows contact with the object, attaches it, lifts, generates place poses, detaches, retreats and returns home.[1] The catch is that the tutorial uses the Franka Panda robot.[1] Your job is to get that pipeline working as-is, then move it onto a UR5e, add your own planning scene, and show with evidence how reliable it is.

From simulation to a real cell. Nothing you verify here is a safety validation. Mock hardware has no physics, Gazebo is an approximation, and the speeds, accelerations and collision margins that work in simulation do not carry straight over to a real robot. A real UR cell would need its own risk assessment, a safety configuration on the robot controller, reduced-speed first runs and the safeguards discussed in 5.4 Making a Robot Cell Safe. Your reflection should name at least two things you would have to check before running your node on real hardware.

By the end you should be able to show a plot of measured RPM against the setpoint, explain every number in your sketch, and show that the FAULT state stops the motor when you hold the wheel or unplug the encoder.

You should also be comfortable with the basic safety ideas from 5.4 Making a Robot Cell Safe: a small motor on a bench is not a robot cell, but the habits of planning for faults and keeping a way to cut power apply at every scale.

The current mismatch you must design around. The 37D motor draws 5.5 A at stall.[5] That is far above the TB6612FNG carrier's 1 A continuous and 3 A peak rating.[6] Every 12 V variant of this motor family stalls at 5.5 A, whatever the gear ratio.[12] So the project must either prevent long stalls (the FAULT state does this in software), limit current at the supply, choose a smaller motor, or use a driver with a higher current rating. Write down which option you chose in your Milestone 0 plan.

A 12 V gearmotor looks harmless, but a geared output shaft is strong enough to trap a finger or fling a loose wheel, and a stalled motor can overheat its driver and wiring. These are standard bench practices; your lab's own rules come first.

Clamp and guard the mechanics. Clamp the motor bracket to the bench, tighten the wheel's set screw on the flat of the D-shaft, keep hair, sleeves and cables clear, and wear safety glasses while the wheel turns.

Pins. Connect encoder channels A and B to pins 2 and 3, the two interrupt pins on an Uno.[4] The PJRC Encoder library "counts pulses from quadrature encoded signals" and uses interrupts by default; it performs best when both pins are interrupt pins.[14][15] Pin 3 is also a PWM pin, but you have just used it for the encoder, so put the motor PWM on another PWM-capable pin such as 5, 6, 9 or 10.[16] Power the encoder as the motor's documentation describes and check its supply voltage range before you connect it.

Detecting a stall or a lost encoder. Both look the same from the controller's point of view: the commanded PWM is high but the measured speed is about zero. Start a timer when that condition becomes true and clear it when it stops being true; if it stays true longer than a limit you choose (a few hundred milliseconds is a reasonable starting point), go to FAULT. Choose the PWM threshold from your open-loop table: it should be clearly above the dead zone. Given the stall current, this check is what protects the driver, so test it in M3.
T3 Load disturbance: while in RUN, add a light, fixed drag (for example a felt pad held in a clamp against the wheel, never your hand) and measure how far the speed dips and how quickly it recovers.
T4 Stall fault: with the supply current-limited and a low PWM limit, block the wheel with a fixed stop and show that FAULT is entered within your time limit and PWM goes to 0.

It is a monitor, not a controller. It reads and reports, and it never clears a stop on its own: UR's service manual says robot stops must never be acknowledged and reset automatically; resuming must be a deliberate action by a person.[1] Safety functions stay on the safety-rated paths from 5.4 Making a Robot Cell Safe and 8.4 Safety over the Network.

M1 Robot state: a ROS 2 node that connects to the Dashboard Server stand-in on port 29999, asks robotmode and safetystatus once a second, and publishes the answers on a topic.[4] Hand in: ros2 topic echo output while you trigger and clear the stand-in's protective stop by hand.
Use the same four-level rubric format as 10.1, with one row per milestone (M0 to M5) and two more rows: "the monitor never resets a stop" (pass/fail) and "someone else could run it from your README".

Nav2 does not require a lidar. Its documentation says there is no requirement to use lidar-based collision avoidance, localization or SLAM, and that a vision or depth based positioning system can be equally successful, as long as the standards below are followed.[1]

The global positioning system (GPS, SLAM or motion capture) must, at minimum, provide the map to odom transform.[1] It updates that transform to account for the odometric drift.[1] This is why the map frame jumps: a localization component keeps re-computing the robot pose from sensor observations, which removes drift but causes discrete jumps when new sensor information arrives.[2]
All of Nav2’s servers are lifecycle (managed) nodes: nodes with state machine transitions for bringup and teardown.[1] This helps a ROS system behave deterministically at startup and shutdown.[1]

Reviews of the field group robot programming methods into online programming, where instructions are taught on the physical robot, and offline programming, where the program is built on a computer model.[3] A third approach, block-based visual programming, lets shop-floor operators without programming experience build applications for collaborative and industrial robots.[4]

FANUC iPendant: The iPendant supplied with R-30iB Plus controllers has enhanced screen resolution and processing capability. The optional 4D Graphics feature animates the robot on the pendant in real time and shows process data, safety (DCS, Dual Check Safety, FANUC's position and speed safety monitoring software) zones, and programmed paths.[8]

Second, teaching is done at reduced speed. OSHA guidance states that robot speeds during programming sessions are below 250 mm/s (10 inches per second),[5] and ABB's manual states that in manual reduced speed mode the movement is limited to 250 mm/s.[7] This ceiling gives an operator close to the arm time to release the enabling device or press the emergency stop before a collision.

On Universal Robots e-Series arms, the operator presses the Freedrive button on the teach pendant (or a Freedrive button on the robot) and pulls the arm into the desired position.[14][10] In Freedrive the brakes are released and the joints move with little resistance; resistance increases as the arm approaches a predefined limit or safety plane.[14]

Offline programming (OLP) generates robot programs on a computer instead of on the physical robot, which only stops while the new program is downloaded and tested.[3][6] The programmer works inside a 3D simulation built from CAD models of the robot, tooling, parts, and fixtures; FANUC ROBOGUIDE, for example, imports CAD models to build accurate layouts and uses virtual robots to design and visualize cells.[17]

Industrial robot arms are highly repeatable but not accurate: they return to a taught point very reliably, but their absolute positioning error is larger and depends on the brand and model.[21] ISO 9283 sets out the performance criteria and test methods used to measure properties such as these.[22] If an uncalibrated OLP program is downloaded directly to a real arm, a weld gun programmed to follow a seam may miss the joint or gouge the metal.

Downtime in car plants is very expensive: a 2024 Siemens survey report put the cost of an idle production line at a large automotive plant at $2.3 million per hour, roughly double the 2019 figure.[25] Stopping a body line to teach hundreds of weld spots by pendant would therefore lose a great deal of output, which is why offline programming is attractive there. Conversely, for a small machine shop with one cobot tending a few CNC mills, an OLP licence is hard to justify, and lead-through programming is usually the economical choice.

Programming an industrial robot requires tools that connect high-level task logic with real-time mechanical motion. General software developers write source code in text editors, compile it, and test it on a computer. In robotics, the software must also coordinate physical arms, grippers, safety interlocks, and programmable logic controllers (PLCs), and in a modern robotic cell the PLCs and robot controllers must be integrated with each other.[1]

Two widely used environments illustrate this contrast: ABB RobotStudio, which ABB describes as the world's most used offline programming tool for robotics,[2] and Universal Robots PolyScope, a graphical interface for UR collaborative robots that is designed for users without coding experience.[3]

Operators configure safety planes: virtual walls defined in cell space. Restricting the tool flange prevents the tool flange and attached tool from crossing a safety plane, and the Restrict Elbow option keeps the elbow joint from passing through a plane. Separate limits cap stopping time and the distance the tool or elbow can travel while stopping.[11]

Reduced Mode: Becomes active when the TCP moves beyond a Trigger Reduced plane or when a configured safety input is triggered, for example by a laser area scanner that detects a person. The robot must decelerate to meet the lower reduced limits, which the integrator sets from the risk assessment.[11][12]

Part of the reason is timing. A robot controller is not a desktop computer running ordinary programs whenever it gets around to them. It runs a real-time motion system that must send fresh commands to the arm on a fixed, very short cycle. Universal Robots' e-Series manual, for example, states that the robot must be controlled at 500 Hz, which means the controller has to tell the arm what to do every 0.002 seconds, and that URScript programs are executed in real time in the controller's RuntimeMachine.[2] A vendor language lets the manufacturer run user programs inside that tightly controlled loop.

The following RAPID module is this lesson's own pick-and-place example. It uses only instructions and data types documented by ABB: MoveJ, MoveL, Offs, WaitDI, SetDO, WaitTime, Stop, and the robtarget and tooldata types.[6][1] The tooldata value follows ABB's layout: whether the robot holds the tool (robhold), the tool frame (tframe, a position and a quaternion), and the tool load (tload: mass, center of gravity, and inertia values).[9] The signal names (diPartInPosition and so on) are examples that would have to be configured on a real controller.

Universal Robots' script language, URScript, looks friendlier than RAPID.[2] Functions are defined with def and closed with end, the lines inside a block must be indented, and variables do not need type declarations: the manual states that a variable's type is deduced from its first assignment. If you know Python, the syntax will feel familiar.

Hardware Abstraction: ROS provides the sensor_msgs package, which defines common sensor message formats, so any vendor's sensor can be used as long as its driver publishes those standard messages. A planar lidar, for example, publishes sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan messages, which navigation and mapping packages read directly.[3] In the other direction, the Nav2 controller publishes velocity commands as geometry_msgs/msg/Twist messages on the cmd_vel topic, and a driver for the particular robot base turns those commands into motor signals.[4]

A central master (roscore): In ROS 1, nodes connect to each other directly, but they find each other through a name service called the master (started by roscore), and connection set-up is negotiated over XML-RPC.[1] Every node therefore depends on that one master. The ROS 2 design team noted that multi-robot systems had no standard approach and were “somewhat of a hack on top of the single-master structure of ROS.”[11]
Unreliable networks: ROS 2 set out to “behave as well as is possible when network connectivity degrades due to loss and/or delay,” a situation common for mobile robots on Wi-Fi.[11]

The defining decision of ROS 2 was to build its communication on an existing industry standard: the Data Distribution Service (DDS) from the Object Management Group (OMG), whose current version is 1.4 (2015).[14][12]

Configurable Quality of Service (QoS): DDS QoS settings control reliability and latency per data stream, from behavior close to raw UDP (good for soft real-time data) to TCP-like reliable delivery.[12] In ROS 2 terms, a high-bandwidth camera or lidar stream can use “best effort” delivery and simply drop late data, while a command that must arrive uses “reliable” delivery.

Security (SROS 2): DDS-Security gives each participant an identity from a public key infrastructure with mutual authentication, encrypts traffic (AES-GCM), and enforces access-control policies. SROS 2 is the set of ROS 2 tools that creates the certificates, keystores, and permission files needed to switch this on.[13]

Navigation 2 (Nav2): Nav2 is the professionally supported successor of the original ROS Navigation Stack.[6] It uses a behavior tree to orchestrate its navigation tasks,[16] and its task servers load plugins for planners, controllers, and behaviors; the documentation covers planners such as NavFn and Smac and controllers such as DWB, MPPI, and Regulated Pure Pursuit.[6] Nav2 builds a model of the environment from sensor data and plans around obstacles in it.[6] Its developers tested it by having a robot navigate safely alongside students on a university campus over a marathon-length distance.[16]

ros2_control hardware interface: The hardware interface is implemented with the ros2_control framework. It does not decide how the robot moves by itself; standard controllers such as the JointTrajectoryController (used with MoveIt 2) or a force-mode controller do that, and the interface also exposes force-torque sensor data, speed scaling, and I/O.[20][18]

Dashboard client: A dashboard client talks to the robot's dashboard server and exposes ROS 2 services such as power_on, brake_release, load_program, play, and unlock_protective_stop, so a ROS program can start the robot and clear a protective stop (after its cause is fixed) without using the teach pendant.[20]
Fleet and digital twin unification: Software must run the same way in a physics simulator such as Gazebo (a digital twin of the cell) and on a varied fleet of physical robots.

This list is a starting heuristic, not a standard. A real selection checks the candidate gripper's datasheet against the actual part, and notes which version of the datasheet each number came from. For example, Robotiq revised the specifications in its Hand-E manual in March 2024 “to account for the change in Gripper payload,” so copies of the manual from before and after that revision give different payload figures for the same gripper.[1] This lesson concentrates on vacuum and finger grippers, which you are most likely to meet first.

The force a cup must supply is larger than the part's weight, because the robot accelerates. Robotiq gives the required holding force as FH = m × (g + a) × S for a horizontal cup lifting straight up (the part is picked from above), FH = m × (g + a/μ) × S for a horizontal cup when the force is horizontal (the part is moved sideways and held by friction), and FH = (m/μ) × (g + a) × S for a vertical cup. Here m is the part mass, g is gravitational acceleration, a is the robot's acceleration, μ is the friction coefficient between cup and part, and S is the safety factor.[4] Robotiq recommends a safety factor of at least 1.5 for smooth parts, 2.0 for porous or oily parts, up to 4.0 when the cup face is vertical, and 2.5 or more for fast swinging or swivelling moves.[4]

Worked example. A 2 kg box is picked from above with a horizontal cup. The robot accelerates upward at a = 5 m/s² and the box is smooth, so S = 1.5. Using Robotiq's formula for a horizontal cup lifting straight up, FH = 2 × (9.81 + 5) × 1.5 = 2 × 14.81 × 1.5 ≈ 44 N.[4] To turn that into a cup size, assume, for this exercise only, that the vacuum generator holds a pressure difference of 60 kPa (a real design takes this from the generator's datasheet). The total cup area must then be at least 44 N ÷ 60,000 Pa ≈ 7.4 × 10-4 m², or about 740 mm². Split over two cups, that is about 370 mm² each, and solving A = π(D/2)² gives D ≈ 22 mm per cup.

The vacuum itself comes either from an electric pump or from an ejector (a venturi device that creates vacuum from a flow of compressed air). Piab, an ejector maker, says ejectors generate no heat or vibration and reduce noise, while conceding that they consume a lot of compressed air.[5] How the ejector is built matters for that air bill. In a stamping study at DaimlerChrysler, multistage ejectors used 1.1 SCFM (standard cubic feet per minute, an industrial measure of compressed-air volumetric flow rate) per cycle, up to 78% less than single-stage generators, and an air-saving check valve that shuts off the air once vacuum is reached reduced consumption further.[6] Piab also claims up to 50% lower compressed-air cost for its compact P2010 multistage ejector, which runs from a 26 psi feed.[7] Treat these as vendor figures: no independent comparison of ejectors and pumps was found for this lesson.

Electric grippers also differ in how they talk to the controller. Zimmer's GEP2000 series comes in three sizes, with 10, 13 and 16 mm of stroke per jaw and up to 200, 360 and 500 N of grip force, and each size is offered with plain digital I/O, with a 0-10 V position-feedback signal, or with IO-Link (a standardized digital point-to-point communication protocol connecting sensors and actuators to industrial controllers).[9] A GEP2000-B variant adds detection of a lost workpiece that is reported to the controller.[10] Vention sells a Universal Robots package for the 16 mm Zimmer gripper (125 to 500 N, 24 V, 2 A maximum, 0.02 mm repeatability) aimed at sites with no compressed air.[11] The choice of interface decides what your program can know: a digital-only gripper reports at most "open" or "closed", while an analog or IO-Link version can report where the jaws actually stopped.

Soft grippers use flexible materials that conform to the item. The OnRobot Soft Gripper, for example, has three interchangeable silicone cups and handles small items under 2.2 kg, with a grip size of 10 to 118 mm depending on the cup. It needs no external air supply and is certified for food contact (FDA 21 CFR for non-fatty foods and EC 1935/2004).[12] Its capacity depends on the item's shape, softness and friction.[12] Inflatable soft grippers can handle varied food shapes with forces that do not bruise, although one patent notes that few industrial soft-robotics designs suit washdown or food-contact environments.[13]

The controller does not see the gripper; it has to be told what it carries. Two groups of numbers matter: the TCP (where the working point of the tool is, covered in lesson 1.6) and the payload, meaning the mass of the tool, and later of the tool plus the part, together with the position of its center of gravity (CoG). The controller uses these numbers in its model of the arm's dynamics. If they are wrong, that model is wrong: path accuracy suffers, and on a force-limited cobot the robot may stop for a collision that never happened, or press harder than expected before it reacts to a real one. So a careful program updates the payload at the pick and restores it at the place.

The tool connector matters most for grippers, because it saves running cables along the arm. A UR community wiki written for the CB3 generation, which has the same tool I/O counts, describes an M8 connector with 2 digital inputs, 2 digital outputs and 2 analog inputs. Signals and tool power are at 12 V or 24 V, switched together, with 600 mA available in total. Because the tool voltage is generated locally, an external power supply does not raise that limit.[26] Check the figures for your controller generation in its own manual. The tool outputs can be set to sink current (NPN), source current (PNP) or push-pull with set_tool_digital_output_mode(n, mode), using mode 1, 2 or 3 respectively.[27] Use the mode your gripper's manual specifies.

URScript has separate functions for the control-box I/O and for the tool I/O. The current script manual's Interfaces module lists get_tool_digital_in(n), set_tool_digital_out(n, b) and set_tool_digital_output_mode(n, mode) for the tool connector.[31] For the standard control-box channels, the same module lists get_standard_digital_in(n) and set_standard_digital_out(n, b).[31] A UR forum reply describes the older generic input function as deprecated in favour of these names, so prefer them to the generic get_digital_in and set_digital_out used in lesson 2.3.[32] Tool power is switched with set_tool_voltage, which UR's own driver script calls.[17]

They are this lesson's own illustrative examples and have not been run on a controller, so test them in a simulator (URSim or RobotStudio) before using them on hardware. They assume the following wiring, which you would change to match your gripper: tool output 0 closes the gripper and tool output 1 opens it; standard input 0 is a part-present sensor; tool input 0 is a gripper-closed-on-part (or vacuum-OK) signal.

In a production cell, the robot is rarely in charge. A programmable logic controller (PLC) usually owns the sequence, and the robot acts as a device that exchanges ready, busy and done bits with it. In the common pattern, permissives such as "E-stop OK" and "guard door closed" come from a safety PLC, safety relays or a safety protocol, not from ordinary I/O. The PLC holds cycle-start on until the robot acknowledges; the robot reports busy and then complete; the PLC acknowledges, and the bits reset.[40] The PLC side is often written as a state machine: a start button and part-present together begin the cycle, and the next state is entered only after the robot reports, for example, position OK and gripper closed. Typical causes of failure are differing PLC and robot cycle times, hard-coded timing delays, and missing checks that both controllers agree on the current state.[41]

Add a "wait for part-present" loop on standard input 0 with a 10 s timeout using sync() and get_steptime(). Run it once with the input off and confirm the popup appears after about 10 s; then toggle the input in the simulator's I/O tab and confirm the robot continues.

The rule for pick-and-place is simple: stop exactly wherever the gripper changes state. The approach and retract points can be blended, but the grip point and the release point must be exact stops. The industrial examples all do this, with a blended zone on the approach and fine on the grip point.[1][2] On ABB's forum, a user's parts were landing in the wrong place, and an experienced user traced it to a blended zone (z100) at the drop point and advised fine.[30] A blend at the grip point means the gripper starts closing while the robot is still moving or cutting the corner.

Wrist singularity: on a UR, a wrist singularity happens when wrist 2 lines up with the plane of the shoulder, elbow and wrist 1, and it can happen anywhere in the workspace.[33] UR's manual warns that the arm can stop or make sudden fast movements near a singularity.[34] A straight-line move that cannot be done often shows up as a joint-limit error, and the fix is to move or add waypoints.[35] Laying out the task differently, tilting the tool, or using a joint move when a straight line is not needed all help.[33]

Build the cycle in the program tree, with waypoints relative to the plane: a joint move to the approach point above the pick, a linear move down to the grip point with no blend (an exact stop), a Set node for the tool output plus a 0.5 s Wait, a linear retract back up, a joint transfer move to above the place point, then the place sequence (linear down, exact stop, open, wait, linear up). Run it with the speed slider turned down. URSim lets you watch the tool output change on the I/O tab.

One idea runs through the lesson. At every point where something can fail, a good program has the same three answers: retry automatically a limited number of times, then tell the operator what is wrong, then stop in a safe, known state.

A practical rule: CONST for numbers that never change, such as pallet spacing; PERS for taught points, tool data and anything that must survive a restart, such as a cycle counter; VAR for scratch values inside one routine.

UR's External Control script works this way. When a target breaks a limit, it shows a non-blocking operator message, popup(str, title="External Control speed limit", blocking=False, warning=True), writes to the log with textmsg(...), and uses a counter, violation_popup_counter, so the popup does not repeat endlessly. When it has to give up, it calls a short routine that slows the robot down before ending the program:[3]

A popup is not a safety function. Users on UR's forum point out that a popup followed by halt cannot be resumed, and a popup without halt does not stop the program at all; for real safety behavior they are directed to the configured safety functions, such as a protective stop, rather than script messages.[26] UR does document a protective_stop() script function, and UR's error code C209 reads "A protective stop was triggered (for test purposes only)".[27][28] Error handling keeps production running and tells people what went wrong; it does not protect people. Guarding, safety-rated stops and safety I/O do that, as covered in 5.4 Making a Robot Cell Safe.

The counter is the part that makes restarts work. Because nPlaced is PERS, it keeps its value even if the program is stopped and started from the beginning,[5] so after a stop at slot 5 the loop resumes at slot 5 instead of stacking a part on slot 0. It is written only after a successful place. The FOR loop's counter i is declared by the FOR statement itself and needs no declaration.

Vision systems for robot guidance are grouped by how much of the part's pose they measure. A 2D system works only in the image plane, with height and width but no depth.[1] It also struggles when parts have little contrast against their background.[2] A 2D result gives the part's X and Y position plus its rotation about the vertical axis.[3] Height and tilt must come from somewhere else: the program assumes the part lies flat on a known, taught plane. FANUC's training material calls this plane the offset frame, the plane in which the part moves, and stresses that the correct part Z height must be set for 2D results to be accurate.[4]

Cognex adds a condition that applies to every method in this lesson: the calibration is valid only while the optics and mounting stay unchanged, and it must be redone if either changes.[14] A bumped bracket, a refocused lens or a new zoom setting all break it. Lock the lens rings and pin the camera mount after calibrating.

Apply that to a typical cell. A camera 1280 pixels wide viewing a 320 mm field gives 4 pixels per millimetre, or 0.25 mm per pixel, so with the 2 to 4 pixel rule the smallest feature it can locate reliably is about 0.5 to 1 mm. Halve the FOV to 160 mm and each pixel covers half as much. That is why a wrist camera that moves closer can see finer detail than a fixed camera that must see the whole table.

In URSim or RobotStudio (see 2.6), create a user frame or work object with its origin at (200, 150) and axes parallel to the original frame, and teach the pick point in it (it should read (10, 0)). Move the frame's origin to (215, 140), rotate it 30° about its own Z axis, and check that the robot now goes to (223.660, 145.000) in the original frame. Test this in the simulator first, never on a real cell.

Framework (the “plumbing”): Messaging, standard interfaces and support for several programming languages, so that, for example, a camera can send images to a processing node or a planner can send commands to a motor controller. Its basic parts are nodes, interfaces (topics, services and actions), parameters and client libraries.[1]

Splitting a robot into small nodes also helps when things go wrong. Because nodes can run as separate processes,[9] a crash in the camera driver (for example, after a USB glitch) does not have to take down the motor controller or a safety monitor running in other processes, and the driver can be restarted on its own without rebooting the robot.

Strict Message Typing: Every field in a ROS message has a type that is enforced, and message types are described in .msg files.[11][13] For example, the standard sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan message holds a header with a timestamp, the start and end angles of the scan, the angle increment between beams, and arrays of ranges and intensities.[14]

A topic gives no built-in acknowledgment that the job is done. A service is the wrong tool too: the documentation says services are expected to return quickly because the client is generally waiting, and should never be used for long-running processes that might need to be preempted, for example if a person walks in front of the robot.[15]

In ROS 2, parameters belong to the individual node that uses them, and their lifetime is tied to that node.[23][22] By default a node must declare every parameter it accepts, and each parameter value has one of a fixed set of types: bool, int64, float64, string, byte[], or arrays of bool, int64, float64 or string. A parameter's descriptor can also hold a description and a valid value range.[23] Parameters can be changed on the command line with ros2 param set, and saved to or loaded from YAML files.[24] Nodes can register callbacks that check or react to parameter changes while running, so values such as controller gains can be tuned without restarting the process.[23]

ROS 2's default middleware is DDS, and nodes find each other automatically through that middleware: a new node advertises itself to other nodes in the same ROS domain, and they reply with information about themselves.[25][26] DDS discovery uses multicast, so the network interface must have multicast enabled.[27]
Why is an asynchronous, decoupled node architecture safer for an industrial robot than running all motor drivers and computer vision logic inside a single monolithic loop?

Multi-Robot Headaches: Multi-robot systems were possible in ROS 1, but there was no standard approach, and the ROS team described them as “all somewhat of a hack on top of the single-master structure of ROS.”[1]

ROS 2 solves this by introducing Quality of Service (QoS) policies, which let a connection be “as reliable as TCP or as best-effort as UDP.” QoS profiles can be set independently for each publisher, subscription, service server and client.[14] The main policies are:[14]

Moving out of a primary state (except after an error in Active) requires an action from an external supervisory process, through transitions such as configure, activate, deactivate, cleanup and shutdown.[17] A supervisor can therefore bring every sensor driver to Inactive first and activate the cell only once each driver reports its hardware ready. That way, hardware is used only when it is ready and is released safely on shutdown.[16][17]

Built-in Security (SROS 2): ROS 2 can secure communication between nodes: it can encrypt data in transit, authenticate the participants sending data, check data integrity and enforce domain-wide access controls.[22] These services come from the security plugins defined by the OMG DDS Security specification, and identities are managed with certificates signed by an identity certificate authority.[22]

That transition period is now over. ROS Noetic Ninjemys, the last ROS 1 distribution, was marked End-of-Life (EOL) on May 31, 2025; after the final sync on May 29, no new Noetic changes were accepted and regressions in binary packages could no longer be fixed.[25][26] ROS 1 has reached the end of development with no new releases planned, while ROS 2 releases a new distribution every year.[26]
