Keep the teleop terminal active and press the arrow keys. Up and Down drive the turtle forward and backward; Left and Right turn it. The turtle draws its path with an attached "pen". Each key press moves it only a short distance before it stops, because a robot should not keep carrying out an old command if, for example, the operator loses the connection.[1] In the Turtlesim source code, the turtle stops if no new velocity command has arrived for one second.[2]

Our class inherits from rclpy.node.Node, and super().__init__ gives the node its name. create_publisher declares that the node publishes Twist messages on a topic with a "queue size" of 10, a Quality of Service setting that limits how many messages are queued if a subscriber cannot keep up. create_timer makes a callback run every 0.5 seconds. In main, the ROS client library is initialised, the node is created, and rclpy.spin(node) keeps the node running so its callbacks are called, until you stop it with Ctrl+C.[13] The Jazzy version of the tutorial writes main in an older style (rclpy.init(), rclpy.spin(), then destroy_node() and rclpy.shutdown()), which you will also see in many existing projects.[14] Because the 0.5 s timer is shorter than Turtlesim's one-second command timeout, the turtle never stops between messages.[2]

Steering a cartoon turtle is a classic beginner exercise, but the same ideas carry over to real robots. For example, diff_drive_controller, the standard wheeled-robot controller in ros2_control, takes velocity commands on a ~/cmd_vel topic as geometry_msgs/msg/TwistStamped (a Twist with a timestamp and frame header) and publishes the robot's odometry on ~/odom as nav_msgs/msg/Odometry.[15] The node, publisher, subscriber and timer patterns you wrote here are the same rclpy patterns the official tutorials teach for any ROS 2 node.[13]

tf2 stores the relationships between frames as a tree, buffered in time, and can transform points and vectors between any two frames at any desired time.[7] In RViz the most important setting is the Fixed Frame, the frame treated as the "world": usually map or world, though it can also be the odometry frame. For correct results, the fixed frame should not move relative to the world. If you set it to a moving frame such as the robot's base, everything the robot has seen will appear in front of the robot instead of where it really is.[1] Each display also shows a status (OK, Warning, Error or Disabled), which is the first place to look when data does not appear.[1]

The documentation defines a workspace simply: "A workspace is a directory containing ROS 2 packages."[3] Workspaces are built in layers. Your ROS 2 installation in /opt/ros/lyrical is the underlay. Your own workspace is an overlay, "a secondary workspace where you can add new packages without interfering with the existing ROS 2 workspace that you're extending." The underlay must contain the dependencies of every package in the overlay, and packages in the overlay override packages with the same name in the underlay. Layers can be stacked more than two deep.[3]

The generated setup.cfg is two short sections, [develop] script_dir=$base/lib/turtle_square and [install] install_scripts=$base/lib/turtle_square. They put the executables in lib "because ros2 run will look for them there."[9][10] Name, version, description, maintainer and license must match between package.xml and setup.py, so edit both when you fill in the TODO fields.[7]

Three calls do most of the work. self.create_publisher(String, 'topic', 10) declares the message type, the topic name and a queue size of 10; "Queue size is a required Quality of Service (QoS) setting that limits the amount of queued messages if a subscriber is not receiving them fast enough." self.create_timer(0.5, self.timer_callback) runs a callback every 0.5 seconds. self.create_subscription(String, 'topic', self.listener_callback, 10) registers a callback that is called "as soon as it receives a message", so a subscriber needs no timer. The topic name and type must match on both sides.[10]

The simplest way to draw a square is open-loop: drive forward for a fixed time, turn for a fixed time, and repeat four times, without ever checking where the turtle actually is. The timeout from Section 07 decides the structure. We cannot send one "go forward" message and sleep; we must keep publishing. So the node uses a timer that fires 10 times a second (every 0.1 s, well under the 1.0 s timeout) and a small state machine with three states: FORWARD, TURN and DONE.[14][10]

The turtle should trace four sides and stop, and Terminal 2 should log "Finished side 1" through "Finished side 4". In a third terminal you can watch it work with ros2 topic echo /turtle1/pose, check who is connected with ros2 topic info /turtle1/cmd_vel, or open rqt_graph from lesson 4.5. To clear the drawing and put the turtle back in the centre, call ros2 service call /reset std_srvs/srv/Empty; if that type is rejected, check it with ros2 service type /reset.[14]
The same idea matters on a factory floor: if a critical driver process dies, you usually want the rest of the system to stop cleanly rather than keep running with stale data.

The second argument to declare_parameter is the default value, which also fixes the parameter's type; changing a declared parameter's type at runtime fails unless it was declared with dynamic typing allowed.[13][3] If a node you write in lesson 4.6 should read a value from a YAML file, it must declare that parameter first.

A node can also guard its own parameters with callbacks. A pre-set callback can modify the list of parameters being set, an on-set callback can inspect a proposed change and explicitly reject it, and a post-set callback reacts after a change has been accepted.[3] That is how a motor driver could refuse a speed limit outside its safe range.

Pilz limits come from two places. The joint_limits.yaml in the MoveIt config overrides the URDF limits, and acceleration limits can only be set there. Cartesian limits for LIN and CIRC (max_trans_vel, max_trans_acc, max_trans_dec, max_rot_vel) go in pilz_cartesian_limits.yaml.[30] UR's file sets a maximum translational velocity of 1.0, acceleration of 2.25, deceleration of -5.0 and rotational velocity of 1.57, and its Pilz pipeline uses PTP as the default planner.[29] Pilz can also chain moves into a MotionSequenceRequest with a blend_radius, so the tool rounds a corner instead of stopping, much like a zone or blend on an industrial controller. If any command in a sequence fails to plan, none are executed.[30]

A simple rule for a pick: use OMPL or PTP to get to a safe pose above the part when you care about avoiding obstacles more than the path shape, and use LIN for the short final approach, where the tool must travel straight down. That is the same MoveJ-then-MoveL pattern from 2.6.

Universal Robots maintains its own ROS 2 driver, built on the Universal_Robots_Client_Library. It works with all UR robots from 3 kg to 30 kg payload on PolyScope X, PolyScope 5 and CB3 controllers, and it supports pausing at an emergency stop or safeguard stop, "automatic speed scaling to avoid violate the safety setting" and manual speed scaling from the teach pendant.[18] Its release table lists Humble, Jazzy, Kilted, Lyrical and Rolling, and the README states that "a fundamental requirement for the driver is using Linux".[18] It is one of the few drivers already released for ROS 2 Lyrical: the Lyrical distribution file lists ur_robot_driver version 6.2.0-1 with its calibration, controller, dashboard, MoveIt configuration and driver packages.[7]

Speed scaling. The robot may run slower than the PC asked, because the pendant speed slider is turned down or because the controller is slowing the arm to stay within its safety settings. The driver multiplies the RTDE values speed_scaling (the slider) and target_speed_fraction (the controller's own slowdown) and publishes the result, from 0 to 1, through the speed_scaling_state_broadcaster.[27] The trajectory controller uses that factor to stretch time so the robot does not fall behind its plan.

MotoROS2 offers a follow_joint_trajectory action, so it fits the common pattern, but it is a trajectory-forwarding driver with clear limits. Before sending a goal, a client must check robot_status, make the trajectory start at the robot's current state ("MotoROS2 will reject any trajectory which does not start at the current state") and call start_traj_mode. A trajectory may hold at most 200 points, state publishing is capped at about 100 Hz, and there is no Cartesian motion, no asynchronous multi-group motion and not yet any replacing of a trajectory while it runs.[11]

The more important point is about safety. ROS 2 is not the robot's safety system. The certified safety functions, such as the safety configuration, emergency stops, protective stops, speed limits and zone limits, live in the vendor's controller and keep working whatever the PC sends. ROS only sends requests, and the robot may slow down or stop at any time. The drivers make this visible:

UR: the driver pauses at emergency and safeguard stops and scales speed to respect the safety settings.[18] The io_and_status_controller publishes the safety mode (for example PROTECTIVE_STOP or ROBOT_EMERGENCY_STOP) and whether the robot program is running; if it is not, "no commands can be sent to the robot".[27]

Your ROS application must cope with the safety system, not fight it; turning off MoveIt's execution monitor on UR robots (section 04) is one example. As a general rule, your risk assessment should assume that ROS commands can be wrong, and rely on the controller's safety functions and the cell safeguards from lesson 5.4 to keep people safe.

In robotics, the ethical stakes are physical and immediate. OSHA's guidance on industrial robots describes how a moving arm can strike a worker, or crush and trap a worker against a post or fixture, and how a single bypassed safeguard has led to deaths.[2] As robots leave fenced cells to work beside people, and mobile robots move through shared spaces, more of an engineer's everyday technical decisions affect whether people stay safe.

I. Integrity and responsible conduct: Members commit to hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public, to protect the privacy of others, and to disclose promptly factors that might endanger the public. They also commit to improve public understanding of conventional and emerging technologies, including intelligent systems, to avoid real or perceived conflicts of interest whenever possible, and to maintain their technical competence.[4]

II. Fair treatment and respect: Members commit to treat all persons fairly and with respect, and not to engage in discrimination or in harassment of any kind, including sexual harassment or bullying.[4][3]

III. Upholding the code: Members commit to strive to ensure the code is upheld by colleagues and co-workers, to support them in following it, and not to retaliate against individuals who report a violation.[4][3]

A central part of engineering ethics is handling conflicts of interest. The NSPE code says to disclose them: "Engineers shall disclose all known or potential conflicts of interest that could influence or appear to influence their judgment or the quality of their services."[1] The IEEE code adds a duty to avoid real or perceived conflicts of interest whenever possible.[4]

A conflict of interest exists whenever an engineer's personal, financial or other business interests could bias their technical judgment, or appear to. For example, suppose a robotics integrator is hired to choose the best vision system for an inspection line, and the lead engineer secretly owns shares in one of the competing sensor start-ups. The engineer can no longer act as an impartial trustee for the client. Hiding the conflict, or ignoring it because the contract is small, breaks the disclosure rule that sits under Canon 4 (faithful agent) and risks a deceptive act under Canon 5.[1] The right response is to disclose the relationship in writing and step back from the vendor evaluation.

Similarly, Canon 2 obliges engineers to work only within their areas of competence.[1] An engineer trained only in computer-vision software should not sign off on the structural welds or the emergency-stop circuits of a heavy industrial manipulator without involving qualified mechanical and safety specialists.

A key idea in the 2025 revision is that collaboration belongs to the application, not to the robot alone. The terms "collaborative robot" and "collaborative operation" no longer appear in ISO 10218; the standard speaks of "collaborative applications" instead.[8][7] The revision also folded in the collaborative-application content of ISO/TS 15066, made functional safety requirements more explicit, and added cybersecurity requirements that relate to robot safety.[8][7] In practice, a robot arm with rounded edges and torque sensing can still be part of a dangerous application if it carries a sharp sheet of laser-cut steel or a cutting torch, so the whole application (robot, end-effector, workpiece and surroundings) must be risk-assessed.
4. Power and force limiting (PFL): Contact between robot and person is allowed, but the robot's speed, force and power are limited so that a contact stays below set biomechanical limits.[2][10]

To make power and force limiting measurable, ISO/TS 15066 gives a table of biomechanical limits. They come from a pain-onset study (project FP-0317) at the University of Mainz with 100 healthy adult volunteers, and they cover 29 specific body areas grouped into body regions.[10][11] For each body region the specification gives a maximum permissible force for quasi-static contact (clamping or crushing where a body part can be trapped); separate pressure limits (in N/cm²) are given for the specific body areas.[12][10]

When do industrial robot accidents actually happen? Studies cited by OSHA, from Sweden and Japan, found that many robot accidents do not occur under normal operating conditions, but during programming, program touch-up and maintenance, and while workers are first exposed to a new application during installation and testing.[2] A NIOSH analysis of US data found 41 robot-related deaths at work from 1992 to 2017. In 78% of them a robot struck the worker while moving under its own power, and many of these strikes happened during robot maintenance.[13]

Most serious robot accidents happen during non-routine work (programming, maintenance, repair, setup and testing) rather than during normal automatic production, when guards and interlocks keep people out of the robot's reach.[2][13]

This is why OSHA expects hazardous energy to be controlled under its lockout/tagout (LOTO) rule, 29 CFR 1910.147 (or 1910.333 for electrical work).[2] Before a technician services equipment inside the robot's space, every energy source (electrical supply, compressed air and stored energy such as gravity on a raised axis) is isolated, locked and tagged.

Autonomous mobile machinery: An autonomous machine may have a supervisor. The machine must send information and alerts to the supervisor, who must be able to stop it, restart it, or move it to a safe position, and the machine must operate safely within a defined working area.[16]

Self-evolving behaviour: When machine learning is used to ensure safety functions, machinery and safety components with self-evolving behaviour require third-party assessment by an independent designated organization, called a notified body. The risk assessment must cover how the machine may behave after it is placed on the market, and data on safety-related decisions must be recorded.[16][15]

The rules for AI in machinery changed again in 2026. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the "Digital Omnibus on AI," published 24 July 2026) moved the Machinery Regulation from Section A to Section B of Annex I of the EU AI Act. The AI Act's detailed high-risk requirements will instead be written into the Machinery Regulation through delegated acts, which the Commission must adopt by 2 August 2028 at the latest.[17]

Strict product liability: In US law, product liability is generally a strict liability matter: once a plaintiff shows the product was defective, the defendant is liable whether or not it took great care. Defects are usually grouped as design defects, manufacturing defects, and marketing defects (poor instructions or failure to warn).[18][19] For example, a collaborative cell whose pinch points exceed the ISO/TS 15066 limits could be argued to have a design defect.

The duty to speak up: Under the NSPE code, if engineers' judgment is overruled in circumstances that endanger life or property, they "shall notify their employer or client and such other authority as may be appropriate," and they shall approve only engineering documents that conform to applicable standards.[1] The IEEE code likewise requires members to disclose promptly factors that might endanger the public.[4] In a US workplace, an appropriate authority can be OSHA.

During final commissioning, the lead safety engineer finds an intermittent fault: when an autonomous pallet jack enters the collaborative zone, the laser area scanner sometimes fails to switch the robot into reduced speed, because of sunlight glinting off the polished concrete floor.

Under the Fundamental Canons, the engineer must refuse.[1] Signing a safety compliance document for a cell with a known, unresolved sensing failure would breach Canon 1 (public safety), Canon 3 (truthful statements) and Canon 5 (deceptive acts), and the rule that engineers approve only documents that conform to applicable standards.[1] The $25,000 daily penalty is real, but the duty to protect human life comes first.

Read the case study above. If you were the junior engineer on that project and your manager pressured you to sign off on the unsafe cell, what specific steps would you take under the NSPE and IEEE codes of ethics?

In ordinary software, an unhandled exception or a deadlock crashes a process or corrupts a record. In robotics, a software bug or a bypassed interlock can let a heavy steel arm move while a person is within reach, and OSHA's accident cases show workers struck, or crushed against posts and fixtures, in exactly this way.[1] Physical safety is therefore not just a compliance checkbox: it is the first ethical obligation an engineer owes to the people who share space with a machine.

The core standard for industrial robots is ISO 10218, revised in 2025 in two parts: ISO 10218-1:2025 covers the industrial robot itself, and ISO 10218-2:2025 covers industrial robot applications and robot cells.[2][3] In the United States, ANSI and A3 published ANSI/A3 R15.06-2025, adapted from both parts.[4] The 2025 revision greatly increased the number of safety functions it describes and made functional safety requirements more explicit.[4][5] A useful way to think about this is defense in depth: physical safeguards, dedicated safety controllers, and supervisory software layers, each able to stop the robot if the others fail.

For machinery, the main functional safety standard is ISO 13849-1:2023, which gives a method for designing the safety-related parts of control systems, including their software.[10] It rates each safety function with a Performance Level from PL a (lowest) to PL e (highest), defined by its probability of a dangerous failure per hour; for PL e this is between 10−8 and 10−7 per hour.[11] The PL achieved depends on the architecture category (B, 1, 2, 3 or 4), the reliability of the parts, the diagnostic coverage and protection against common-cause failures.[12] Robot safety controllers are commonly certified to PL d, Category 3, as the ABB and Universal Robots examples below show.[13][14]

A watchdog is a hardware counter that counts down from a starting value to zero. The software must restart it regularly ("kick the dog") before it reaches zero. If the software hangs, it stops kicking, the counter reaches zero and the watchdog acts: in a simple embedded system it resets the processor.[16] In a robot, the watchdog output can be wired into the safety circuit, so that a hung control program also removes the robot's permission to move and brings it to a Category 0 or Category 1 stop.

ABB SafeMove: Supervises tool position against defined zones, tool orientation, tool speed and standstill, using a two-channel safety controller in the robot controller that checks the main computer's motion data. ABB states that it complies with PL d under ISO 13849-1.[13]

Universal Robots safety system: Provides joint position and speed limits, a tool (TCP) speed limit, force and momentum limits, and up to eight safety planes, certified to PL d, Category 3 by TÜV Rheinland.[14]

In December 2022, an MIT Technology Review investigation found that some of the contract workers labeling images taken inside homes by development Roomba robots had shared them in private online groups; 5.3 covers the case.[18]

In a landmark 2018 study, Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested commercial gender-classification systems and found that darker-skinned women were the most misclassified group, with error rates of up to 34.7%, while the maximum error rate for lighter-skinned men was 0.8%.[20] Similar problems matter for robots and vehicles that must detect people in order to avoid them:

Pedestrian detection disparities: A 2023 test of eight deep-learning pedestrian detectors found that the proportion of undetected children was 20.14% higher than for adults, and found significant gender bias at night.[21]

Interaction across diverse users: Service robots that read faces or gestures may work less well for groups that were under-represented in their training data, which is the pattern the Gender Shades study revealed for face analysis.[20]

Engineers therefore have a responsibility to audit training data, measure detection errors separately for different groups of people, and avoid relying on a single camera-based model for safety-critical person detection.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) describes autonomous weapon systems as systems that select and apply force to targets without human intervention: after activation, they strike in response to sensor data matching a general "target profile."[24] The main concerns raised against them are:

Accountability gap: Human Rights Watch and Harvard Law School's International Human Rights Clinic argue that programmers, manufacturers and military personnel could all escape liability for unlawful deaths caused by a fully autonomous weapon, and that commanders often could not foresee or prevent such an attack.[25]

Campaigners use the phrase meaningful human control for the level of human judgment they believe must be kept over the use of force.[25] The ICRC has recommended new legally binding rules: prohibiting unpredictable autonomous weapons and those designed or used to apply force against persons, and limiting all others, including requirements for human supervision with timely intervention and deactivation.[24] Existing law already requires states party to Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions to review any new weapon, means or method of warfare during its study, development, acquisition or adoption (Article 36).[26]

Ethical requirements and risk-based design: Turning those values into requirements and tracing them through the concept of operations (a document describing how the system is intended to operate in its working environment) into the system design, with attention to harms to values as well as physical harm.[27][29]

This applies to industrial machinery and collaborative robots: under the EU AI Act, an AI system that is a safety component of a product covered by EU product-safety law listed in Annex I, such as machinery, is classified as high risk when that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that law. High-risk systems come with requirements for risk management, data governance, logging and human oversight.[28][30] In 2026, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the "Digital Omnibus on AI") changed how this works for machinery: the Machinery Regulation moved to Section B of Annex I, so only a few AI Act articles (including the Article 6(1) classification) apply directly, and the detailed high-risk requirements will be added to the Machinery Regulation through delegated acts due by 2 August 2028. High-risk rules for AI in other regulated products apply from 2 August 2028.[31][30] By combining hardware safety with this kind of governance, engineers can make autonomous machines that serve people without sacrificing their safety or dignity.

Inspect a commercial robotic device (such as a robotic lawn mower, an automated warehouse AMR, or a 3D printer) and identify its hardware safety controls, including physical stops, interlocks, and presence sensors.

Diagram a dual-channel safety circuit containing an emergency stop button, an enabling switch, and a safety PLC, explaining how a single broken wire is detected without disabling the safety stop function.

Daron Acemoglu (MIT) and Pascual Restrepo (Boston University) carried out a benchmark study of the employment effects of industrial robots, published in the Journal of Political Economy in 2020.[2] They compared US commuting zones (local labor markets) with different exposure to robots, measured from industry-level advances in robotics and each area's mix of industries. They showed that the areas most exposed to robots after 1990 had no different trends before then, and that the impact of robots was distinct from that of other capital and technologies.[2]

Studying US labor markets from 1990 to 2007, Acemoglu and Restrepo found that one more robot per thousand workers reduced the employment-to-population ratio by 0.2 percentage points and wages by 0.42%.[2]

The size of the estimate changed between versions of the study. The 2017 working paper gave a range of 0.18 to 0.34 percentage points for employment and 0.25 to 0.5 percent for wages, and its summary described the arrival of one new robot in a local labor market as coinciding with an employment drop of 5.6 workers.[3] Headline numbers like these are averages across many regions; they describe exposed local labor markets, not every worker or every country.

To explain why automation affects labor in more than one way, Acemoglu and Restrepo set out a task-based framework in the Journal of Economic Perspectives.[4] Instead of treating production as a mix of abstract "capital" and "labor," the framework treats it as a set of tasks (such as machining parts, routing circuit boards, scheduling logistics and troubleshooting errors), each of which can be done by people or by machines.[4]

1. The displacement effect: Machines take over tasks that people used to do. Automation always reduces labor's share of value added (the net economic output generated after deducting intermediate material costs), and it may reduce the demand for labor even while it raises productivity.[4] For example, replacing manual spot-welders with robot arms removes the welding task from human workers.

Whether automation helps or harms overall employment depends on the balance between these effects. Acemoglu and Restrepo's decomposition of US data attributes slower employment growth over the last three decades to three causes: an acceleration of the displacement effect, especially in manufacturing; a weaker reinstatement effect; and slower productivity growth than in earlier decades.[4]

Source: IFR, World Robotics 2024.[5] China's density rose from 402 in 2022 to 470 in 2023, overtaking Germany and Japan, and the IFR attributes this to the country's push to use automation technology.[5] Density figures show where robots are used most, but on their own they do not tell us what robots do to jobs and wages; that question needs studies such as Acemoglu and Restrepo's, which compare places with different exposure over time.[2]
A further 32% are likely to change significantly: These jobs have a probability of automation between 50% and 70%, so many of their tasks could change even if the job itself remains.[7][6]

A central consequence of automation so far has been labor market polarization rather than the disappearance of work. David Autor describes how, in recent decades, wage gains in the United States went disproportionately to workers at the top and the bottom of the income and skill distribution, not to those in the middle.[8] Computers substitute most easily for workers in routine, codifiable tasks, while they amplify the advantage of workers who supply problem-solving skills, adaptability and creativity. Autor also argues that this polarization is unlikely to continue very far into the future.[8]

Reducing the human cost of this transition takes deliberate investment in apprenticeships, retraining and adult education. Engineers can help too: a robot cell that operators can retool, troubleshoot and reprogram (for example through lead-through teaching or simple graphical programming) creates skilled work around the robot instead of only removing tasks.

The severity of these risks was highlighted in December 2022, when MIT Technology Review reported that development versions of iRobot's Roomba J7 series had taken intimate photographs inside homes in 2020, including one of a woman on the toilet.[9] The images were sent to Scale AI, whose contract workers in Venezuela labeled them to train the robot's AI, and some of those workers posted them in private groups on Facebook, Discord and other platforms.[9] iRobot said the images came from special development robots given to paid data collectors and employees who had signed written agreements acknowledging that video and other data would be sent back for training.[9]

The incident shows that robot data can flow through long, multi-company supply chains. Even when the people who own or test a device have signed an agreement, others who appear in the images have not, and contractors and cloud pipelines can expose private moments far from where they were recorded.[9]

The main defense is data minimization. Article 5(1)(c) of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requires that personal data be "adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed."[10] The IEEE Code of Ethics also lists protecting the privacy of others as a duty.[11]

For a robot vacuum's camera, data minimization means that you collect only what the task needs, process it on the robot when possible and keep it no longer than necessary, and tell people clearly what is recorded.[10]

When a manually controlled machine causes an injury, it is often fairly clear who is responsible. When an autonomous system causes harm, responsibility is spread across many people: the perception software engineer, the people who prepared the training data, the systems integrator, the company that deployed the system and the operator on shift.[12]

In 2019, Madeleine Clare Elish of the Data & Society Research Institute introduced the idea of a moral crumple zone to describe how responsibility for an action may be misattributed to a human actor who had only limited control over an automated or autonomous system.[12] Just as the crumple zone of a car is designed to absorb the force of a crash, the human operator can end up absorbing the moral and legal blame when the larger system fails.[12]

Elish developed the idea from high-profile accidents involving complex automated socio-technical systems; her sources include the Three Mile Island nuclear accident, the loss of Air France flight 447 and the 2018 crash of an Uber self-driving test vehicle in Tempe, Arizona.[12] In such cases the human operator tends to be blamed for failing to intervene in time, even though people are poorly suited to monitoring an automated system passively for long periods and then taking over at a moment's notice.

Several frameworks can structure this thinking. IEEE 7000-2021 gives a process for eliciting stakeholders' values and tracing them into system requirements.[14] The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) regulates AI by risk: it prohibits some AI practices outright, sets requirements for high-risk systems (risk management, technical documentation and record-keeping, and human oversight) and adds transparency obligations for certain other AI systems.[15] In 2026, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 moved AI in machinery, such as industrial robots, under the EU Machinery Regulation (Annex I, Section B of the AI Act), which is to add the AI requirements through delegated acts by 2 August 2028.[16] Before deploying an autonomous robot into a shared workspace, a public space or a home, ask five questions:
5. Rules: Which safety standards (such as ISO 10218 and ISO 13849) and laws (such as the EU Machinery Regulation and the EU AI Act) apply where it will be used? (See 5.2.)

Draft an architectural proposal for an autonomous drone delivery system that eliminates the "moral crumple zone" by establishing clear algorithmic handoffs and logging mechanisms between autonomous flight software and remote human dispatchers.

Lesson 5.1 introduced the standards behind industrial robot safety (ISO 10218:2025, ISO/TS 15066 and the EU Machinery Regulation) and the accident data that explain why they exist. This lesson is the practical sequel. It follows the steps an integrator takes to turn an unguarded robot on a shop floor into a cell that people can run, teach, clear and repair without being hurt.

Why insist on a task-based list? Because the dangerous moments are rarely normal production. As lesson 5.1 showed, a NIOSH study of 41 robot-related deaths in the United States from 1992 to 2017 found that 78% involved a robot striking a worker, often during maintenance.[10] An assessment that covers only automatic running misses jam clearing, teaching, tool changes, cleaning and repair.

Fences. The height of a fence and its distance from the hazard are set by ISO 13857, whose current edition (2019) was reconfirmed in 2025. It covers people aged 14 and older; the 5th-percentile stature of a 14-year-old is about 1400 mm.[11] The fence maker Troax advises that protective structures lower than 1400 mm should not be used without additional safety measures, and that reach-over distances come from ISO 13857 Table 2, which relates the hazard height, the fence height and the horizontal distance between them.[12] Openings in the fence must be sized under the same standard, so that fingers, arms or a whole body cannot reach through.

Interlocked doors. A door in the fence is fitted with an interlocking device under ISO 14119, so that opening the door stops the robot. ISO 14119 classifies interlocks by type. A Type 4 interlock uses a coded actuator such as an RFID tag or a coded magnet, while a switch with an uncoded actuator, such as an uncoded magnet, is Type 3. Coding levels are low, medium and high, and high coding means more than 1,000 code variations. ISO 14119 sets additional measures against defeat that depend on the device type.[13][14]

A light curtain is a row of infrared beams. When a hand or body breaks the beams, it sends a stop signal. It lets an operator reach in without opening a door, but it only works if it is mounted far enough from the hazard that the robot has stopped before the hand arrives. ISO 13855 gives that minimum distance as:[17][18]

For a light curtain with a resolution d of 40 mm or less, K = 2000 mm/s and C = 8 × (d − 14) mm, with C never below 0. This version is valid for S up to 500 mm. If S calculated with K = 2000 comes out above 500 mm, you recalculate with K = 1600 mm/s, but S must stay at least 500 mm.[17][18]

For coarser curtains (resolutions from 40 to 70 mm), Datalogic gives K = 1600 mm/s and a reach-over allowance of C = 850 mm, with the highest beam at 900 mm and the lowest beam at 300 mm.[18] ReeR gives the same K and C for resolutions of 50 to 90 mm.[19] These rules and examples follow the long-used 2010 edition of ISO 13855, as presented in vendor guides. The current edition, ISO 13855:2024, which replaced the 2010 edition, restates the formula as S = (K × T) + DDS + Z, where DDS takes the place of C and Z is an application-dependent supplement, and it adds new cases such as mobile applications. Check the current text before you position a real safeguard.[20][21]

Every cell needs emergency stop buttons, but they play a specific role. The emergency stop standard ISO 13850 says an emergency stop "shall not be applied as a substitute for safeguarding measures."[22][23] It is a complementary protective measure under Step 2 of ISO 12100, a last line of defense for when something has already gone wrong.

Teach mode is a special case, because a programmer must stand near a powered robot to jog it and record points. Two measures protect them. The first is reduced speed. In the Universal Robots manual, the speed of the tool center point and of the elbow both start limited to 250 mm/s in teach or program mode; the speed slider can raise the limit, but activating the enabling device resets it to 250 mm/s.[26] The second is a three-position enabling device on the pendant. On UR15, UR20 and UR30 robots, manual-mode motion requires holding the enabling button in its center position. Releasing it, or squeezing it fully in a panic grip, stops the robot immediately; UR classes this as a category 2 stop. UR says this three-position-enabling pendant is mandatory for those models under ISO 10218-1:2025.[27] The UR manual also recommends pairing the enabling device with a mode switch wired as a safety input.[26]

A combination of S2, F2 and P2 gives PLr e, the highest level.[6] Consider a door on a cell that operators enter several times an hour (F2), where a fast robot (P2) could cause serious injury (S2): the door's safety function would need PL e. The speed at which the hazardous situation arises is one of the factors for P, so measures such as reduced speed may justify a lower avoidance rating, and therefore a lower PLr.[30] S, F and P choices are judgment calls, so record the reasoning for each one.

The designer then has to show that the safety function as built achieves at least the PLr. The architecture Category (B, 1, 2, 3 or 4) is part of that proof, together with the reliability of the components (MTTFD) and the diagnostic coverage (DC). Categories are not inputs to the risk graph. The 2015 revision of the standard also lets PLr drop by one level if a low probability of occurrence is proven.[29][31] Note that ISO 13849-1:2023 is now the current edition, and it reworks the Annex A guidance on finding PLr, so check which edition your project has to follow.[32][30] In practice, door switches, light curtains and emergency stops are wired into safety-rated inputs on the robot controller or a safety PLC, often with two channels, so that a single fault does not hide a stop demand.

ABB SafeMove: Programmable safe zones, safe speed limits and safe standstill monitoring. ABB's SafeMove application manual states that SafeMove, together with the safety module and the robot controller, complies with PL d under ISO 13849-1, equivalent to Category 3. The PL e certification mentioned in a 2017 SafeMove2 overview belongs to a safety digital input module, not to the whole safety function, so check the documentation for the rating of each function you use.[36][37][38]

ISO 10218-2:2025 makes functional safety requirements "more explicit rather than implied,"[40][41] and adds robot classifications with matching functional safety requirements and test methods.[40] The same revision integrated the collaborative requirements from ISO/TS 15066 and merged guidance on end-effectors and manual load stations from the former TR (Technical Report) 20218-1 and -2.[40][42] The four collaborative modes are described in lesson 5.1. Here the practical point is that they are built from the controller functions above: FANUC's speed check slowing the robot when a person enters is a speed-and-separation use,[34] and UR's speed and force limits are the basis of power and force limiting.[39]

Teaching needs a powered robot, so it relies on reduced speed and the enabling device. Mechanical repair does not need power, so it relies on lockout/tagout (LOTO). In the United States, OSHA's rule 29 CFR 1910.147 applies to servicing and maintenance where unexpected energization, start-up or release of stored energy could injure someone, and its exception for minor servicing is narrow.[43] A3 notes that discussions of robot maintenance quickly turn to LOTO, which removes the hazardous energy source before work begins.[44]

On 21 July 1984, a 34-year-old die-cast operator with 15 years' experience was pinned between the right rear of a hydraulic robot and a safety pole, and went into cardiopulmonary arrest. The robot took castings from a die-cast machine, dipped them in a quench tank and loaded a trim press. NIOSH investigated the death in its Fatality Assessment and Control Evaluation (FACE) report 8420.[47][48]

The robot's measured stopping time grows from 0.1 s to 0.25 s after a heavier gripper is fitted. Using a 14 mm light curtain with a 0.02 s response time, recalculate the safety distance with S = K × T + C, and say what has to change in the cell layout.

Artificial intelligence (AI) now appears in robot cameras, maintenance dashboards and programming tools, and in research models that try to control a robot directly from images and words. The marketing around these products often blurs one important line: helping people build and run a robot cell is different from deciding, in real time, whether the robot is safe to move. This lesson draws that line clearly.

In industry today, AI mostly sits around the robot. It helps the robot see parts, helps engineers predict when a gearbox will fail, and helps programmers write code faster. The safety-rated controller and its safety configuration (the speed limits, safety planes, stop functions and safeguard inputs you met in 5.4) stay conventional and deterministic. They do the same thing every time for the same input, and they have been validated against a standard.

At NVIDIA's GTC conference in March 2025, UR's parent company Teradyne and its partners showed version 1.1 of the AI Accelerator, which integrates NVIDIA Isaac Manipulator components. In one partner demo (from Groundlight), the system "trains a model to detect a workpiece and generate a robot program for picking."[2] At GTC Paris in June 2025, a UR15 arm running PolyScope X picked objects whose positions it was not given in advance, to show how applications built with the AI Accelerator cope with variation; UR reportedly named machine tending and bin picking as target uses.[3]

FANUC's Zero Down Time (ZDT) service "continuously monitors robot condition and performance data to identify potential issues before they impact production," according to FANUC America's product page (launch date not found for this lesson).[4] In March 2025, Siemens extended its Industrial Copilot to maintenance through Senseye Predictive Maintenance, and claimed that pilot users saved "on average 25% reactive maintenance time."[5] That 25% figure is a vendor claim, not an independent study.

As of October 2026, the research for this lesson did not find a Universal Robots or FANUC LLM assistant specifically for writing robot programs, and KUKA and Yaskawa announcements were not searched. The examples in this lesson's exercise therefore use a general-purpose chatbot as the "AI author," not a vendor product.

A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks. In robotics, the most discussed kind is the vision-language-action (VLA) model: it takes camera images and a written instruction ("put the red block in the bowl") and outputs robot actions directly. These models were all released between 2023 and 2026 as research or early-access platforms, not as certified industrial controllers.

The developers of these models are open about their limits, and those limits matter for a factory. OpenVLA's documentation says that "out-of-the-box, it only works well on domains from the training dataset," that adapting it to a new setup typically needs fine-tuning on about 100 demonstrations, and that it "struggles with high-frequency data."[12] NVIDIA warns that GR00T users "may observe 5-6% variance between runs" because of random data augmentation during training.[13] In other words, two training runs on the same data can give noticeably different robots. That is the opposite of the repeatable, validated behaviour a safety function needs.

At USENIX Security 2025, Spracklen and colleagues tested 16 code-writing LLMs on 576,000 generated code samples in Python and JavaScript. The models regularly told programmers to install software packages that do not exist. The average rate of these hallucinated packages was at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models, and the study found 205,474 unique invented package names.[17][18] The authors also reported that mitigation techniques reduced the rate, but did not remove it.[17] A 2026 replication on newer models, not yet peer reviewed, reported rates between 4.62% and 6.10%; treat it as provisional.[19] A hallucination, in this sense, is output that looks confident and plausible but is not grounded in fact.

RoboRepair (2024): Its authors summarise the problem directly: "LLM-generated programs may be faulty, either due to ambiguity in instructions, misinterpretation of the desired task, or missing information about the world state."[24]

Units. URScript uses SI units. The script manual's entry for movel(pose, a=1.2, v=0.25, t=0, r=0) gives acceleration in m/s², speed in m/s, time in seconds and blend radius in metres. Its example pose p[0.2,0.3,0.5,0,0,3.14] means 200, 300 and 500 mm with a 180° rotation, and "v = 0.25 -> velocity of 250 mm/s."[25] UR's support articles say the same thing plainly: X, Y and Z values are in metres, and Rx, Ry and Rz values are in radians.[26] Joint positions passed to movej are also in radians, which is why URScript provides d2r() to convert degrees. One thread on the UR forum points out that the manual's description of the pose type does not state units clearly, and that a third-party wrapper (RoboDK) assumed millimetres.[27] An LLM trained on RAPID examples (which use millimetres, as you saw in 2.3) can easily carry that habit into URScript.

Frames. A pose only means something relative to a frame: the robot base, the tool, or a feature frame on the fixture. URScript's pose_add adds an offset in the base frame, while pose_trans applies an offset expressed in the frame of the first pose, so pose_trans(pick, p[0, 0, -0.05, 0, 0, 0]) means "50 mm back along the tool's own Z axis." Mixing them up is a classic error. When the tool points straight down, its Z axis points the opposite way to the base's Z axis, so an offset meant to back the tool away from a part can instead drive it 50 mm into the part. A wrong tool center point (TCP) setting causes the same kind of silent offset.

Robot safety standards were tightened just as AI tools spread. ISO 10218-1:2025 and ISO 10218-2:2025 are the first major revision of the industrial robot safety standard since 2011, and they replace the 2011 editions. The revision makes functional-safety requirements "more explicit rather than implied," introduces Class I and Class II robots with different functional-safety requirements, moves away from a blanket Performance Level d requirement towards levels chosen by risk assessment, and adds cybersecurity requirements and collaborative-application content that used to sit in ISO/TS 15066.[28][29][30] None of the sources consulted for this lesson says that ISO 10218:2025 addresses machine-learning components specifically.

This gives a simple rule for the classroom and the workplace. An LLM can help write the application program. It must never write, alter or bypass the safety configuration: the safety planes, speed and force limits, emergency stop and safeguard I/O settings. Those settings are password protected on the teach pendant for a reason, and changing them means the cell's risk assessment has to be revisited. If an AI tool suggests muting a safeguard or disabling a protective stop "to avoid interruptions," the correct response is to refuse and to treat everything else it wrote with extra suspicion.

The legal picture in the European Union is still settling, so read this section as a snapshot as of October 2026, based on law-firm and expert summaries rather than on the legal texts themselves. Check the Official Journal and EUR-Lex before relying on any detail.

The Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (introduced in 5.1) lists, in its Annex I Part A, the products that need mandatory third-party conformity assessment (the formal verification process proving that a product complies with statutory safety requirements). That list includes "safety components with fully or partially self-evolving behaviour using machine learning approaches ensuring safety functions," and machinery that embeds such systems.[32][33] Most of the regulation applies from January 2027; most summaries give 20 January 2027, while one secondary source gives 14 January 2027, so confirm the date on EUR-Lex.[32][33] "Self-evolving behaviour" has no formal definition. The Danish Technological Institute works with a practical one: machine-learning software that operates on generalisations it learned from data, during training and during operation.[34] In short, if a learned model performs a safety function, an independent body has to examine it.

The EU AI Act treats an AI system as high-risk when it is a safety component of a product (or is itself a product) covered by EU product legislation that requires third-party conformity assessment.[35] In 2026 the EU changed how that applies to machinery. According to law-firm summaries, a provisional agreement on the "Digital Omnibus on AI" was reached on 7 May 2026 and voted by the European Parliament on 16 June 2026.[36] It was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (firms write the number in different forms, so check the Official Journal)[37] and entered into force on 27 July 2026.[38] It moves the Machinery Regulation from Section A to Section B of the AI Act's Annex I, so AI-enabled machinery is regulated through the Machinery Regulation, whose essential requirements the Commission is to amend by delegated acts. The high-risk obligations for products in Annex I are delayed to 2 August 2028, and those for Annex III uses to 2 December 2027.[38][37]

No source found for this lesson makes an AI vendor responsible for a user's robot program. The structure of conformity assessment points the other way: the manufacturer and the integrator who signs the risk assessment answer for the cell, and the programmer who deploys code answers for that code. This is a reading of how the system is set up, not a legal ruling, but it is the safe way to work. It also connects to the "moral crumple zone" from 5.3: if AI writes the code and a human only presses Play, the human can end up absorbing the blame for a system they did not really control. To avoid that, the human has to actually review the code, not just approve it.

The page How this course was made explains which tools were used and how references were verified. You should read these lessons the way you will read AI-written robot code: follow the citations, notice where a source is marked as unverified, and check anything that would matter if it were wrong. If this course later offers an AI tutor, check its answers in the same way.

High-level robotic architectures such as ROS 2 often run on single-board computers or PCs with a general-purpose operating system like Linux. A standard Linux kernel is not set up as a real-time operating system: the mainline kernel offers several preemption models, and only the "Fully Preemptible Kernel" model turns Linux into a real-time OS. Without it, a time-critical thread can be held up by other work, so its timing is not guaranteed.[1]

Each GPIO pin can supply only a small current, and the limit differs between boards. On the Uno R3, Arduino lists 20 mA per I/O pin, and the ATmega328P's absolute maximum rating is 40 mA per pin; 20 mA is the datasheet's test condition at 5 V, not a safe target to run at continuously.[3][7] On the Uno R4, Arduino states that the RA4M1's GPIOs can handle up to 8 mA and warns never to connect devices that draw more current directly to a GPIO.[5]

Current demands versus pin limits: An Uno R3 pin is listed for 20 mA (absolute maximum 40 mA) and an Uno R4 pin for 8 mA.[3][7][5] Even small DC gearmotors need far more than this when running, and much more again when starting or stalled, so they must be fed from a driver circuit, not from a pin.[11] Check the stall current on your motor's datasheet before choosing a driver.

Autonomous mobile robots need light, energy-dense power sources, so many use rechargeable lithium-based batteries such as Lithium Polymer (LiPo) packs. Lithium-based cells can go into thermal runaway if mistreated (Battery University lists a thermal runaway temperature of about 150 °C for lithium cobalt oxide), so every robotics engineer should know the basic voltage limits.[15] The figures below are for cobalt-based lithium cells; always check your own pack's datasheet.

Nominal cell voltage: Battery University lists a nominal voltage of 3.60 V per cell for lithium cobalt oxide.[15] Cells are wired in series to raise the voltage: a 2S pack has two cells in series and a 3S pack has three, so their nominal voltages are about twice and three times the cell value. Hobby packs are often labelled with a slightly higher nominal value per cell, so read the label.

Maximum charged voltage: Cobalt-blend lithium-ion cells typically charge to 4.20 V per cell with a tolerance of ±50 mV (8.4 V for 2S, 12.6 V for 3S). Prolonged charging above 4.30 V on a cell designed for 4.20 V plates metallic lithium on the anode, and a fully charged cell has a lower thermal runaway temperature than a partly charged one.[16]

PythonRobotics uses the same pair of formulas: it computes θ2 with an arccosine of the law-of-cosines expression and then θ1 = atan2(y, x) − atan2(l2 sin θ2, l1 + l2 cos θ2).[1] The Modern Robotics course materials describe the 2R solution with the same two tools, the two-argument arctangent and the law of cosines.[2] Section 06 explains why this lesson uses atan2 for θ2 instead of an arccosine.

Closed-form IK when the wrist is spherical. Most industrial arms have a spherical wrist: the last three joint axes meet at one point. Course slides and research papers trace closed-form solutions for this case to Pieper's 1968 work on arms with three consecutive axes intersecting at a point.[6] The wrist-centre position then depends only on joints 1 to 3, so IK splits into a position problem (find the wrist centre, with law-of-cosines geometry much like this lesson's elbow) and an orientation problem for joints 4 to 6. Each split brings its own two-way choices, such as elbow up or down and wrist flipped or not. Sources describe up to 8 solutions for this kind of arm; a reference page for the Puma 560 gives 8 “because of the different possible arm configurations”.[6][7] A general 6R arm with no special geometry is reported to have at most 16 solutions.[8] Treat these two counts as reported figures from summaries of the sources; confirm them in a standard robotics textbook.

Numerical IK when there is no closed form. For a general arm, or a 7-axis arm, controllers solve IK numerically. The Modern Robotics library documents its function IKinBody as one that “Uses an iterative Newton-Raphson root-finding method”. It repeats θ ← θ + J+(θ)·error, where J+ is the pseudoinverse of the Jacobian (a generalization of the matrix inverse that calculates minimum-norm joint velocities when the Jacobian is non-square or near singular), until the orientation and position errors are below set tolerances. It needs an initial guess of joint angles that is already close to the target pose, stops after a hard-coded 20 iterations, and reports success = False if it has not converged.[4][5] Peter Corke's Robotics Toolbox for Python offers a numerical IK solver written in C++, robot.ik_LM(Tep), and its README demonstrates it on the 7-axis Franka Panda, then checks the answer by running FK with robot.fkine(q). The README claims numerical IK can be solved “in as little as 4 microseconds”.[9]

Digital microcontroller pins are binary: an output is either fully on (the board's supply voltage, such as 5 V on an Uno or 3.3 V on boards like the MKR family) or fully off (0 V).[1] The physical world robots work in, however, is analog and continuous. A mobile robot rarely drives its motors at only 0% or 100% speed. To turn smoothly, track a line or hold a steady speed down a slope, the controller must command intermediate power levels.

In the Arduino environment, analogWrite(pin, value) controls hardware PWM.[3] Despite its name, analogWrite() does not output an analog voltage on most pins: it makes the pin generate a steady rectangular wave of the chosen duty cycle until the next call.[3] The value runs on a 0 to 255 scale: 255 means always on and 127 means on about half the time.[1] Worked example: commanding an average of 3.0 V from a 5.0 V Arduino pin corresponds to:

What pulse width sent at 50 Hz commands a standard hobby servo to its neutral center position? The answer is 1.5 milliseconds (1500 microseconds).[8][10] Real servos differ: some accept wider pulses, while others hit mechanical limits and can be damaged if driven past them.[8] The Arduino Servo library's write(angle) maps 0° to 180° onto a default pulse range of 544 to 2400 microseconds, starts servos at 1500 microseconds, and refreshes them every 20 milliseconds; writeMicroseconds() sets the pulse width directly.[12]

Inductive Flyback Voltage Spikes: Motor windings are inductors, so abruptly switching off their current produces a voltage spike. H-bridge circuits must give this current a safe path. The L298 datasheet requires an external bridge of fast-recovery diodes (trr of 200 ns or less) when driving inductive loads.[11] MOSFET drivers such as the DRV8833 instead let the recirculating current flow back to the power supply through the output transistors' body diodes (fast decay) or recirculate it through the shorted motor winding (slow decay).[16]

This section is an illustrative design, not a description of a particular product. A robotic parallel gripper shows the value of combining PWM with sensor feedback. If a gripper is driven only by an on/off switch, the fingers close at full speed and force, which can crush delicate objects (such as eggs or fruit) or stall and overheat the motor.

When a robotics engineer writes a program commanding a mobile robot to drive forward for two seconds, or tells a robotic arm joint to power on for 500 milliseconds, the system is running in an open-loop configuration. The microcontroller has sent power to the actuators, but it has no sensor confirmation of what movement actually happened. If the battery voltage drops, if the floor changes from smooth vinyl to thick carpet, or if a wheel hits an obstacle, the robot's real motion will drift away from what was commanded.

Incremental Encoders: An incremental encoder produces a stream of pulses as the shaft turns, so it can only report a change in position; the controller counts pulses relative to wherever it started.[1][3] It keeps no record of its position, so when the power goes off, its position is forgotten and the robot has to home again. After power-up, the system must move to an index or home position to recover its location.[1] Some incremental encoders provide a third index channel (Channel Z) for this, which pulses once per revolution;[4] a counter can reload a known value when the index signal appears.[5]

Absolute encoders are further divided into single-turn and multi-turn devices. A single-turn encoder reports the angle within one 360-degree revolution, while a multi-turn encoder also keeps count of how many full rotations have happened.[1] As an example of typical resolutions, the SSI interface's standard word lengths are 13 bits for single-turn encoders (8,192 positions per turn) and 25 bits for multi-turn encoders.[6] Optical absolute encoders usually code each position in Gray code, in which only one bit changes between neighbouring positions, so a reading taken mid-transition is off by at most one step.[7]

If a program tries to catch these transitions by polling the encoder pins with digitalRead() inside loop(), it must check the pins constantly to avoid missing pulses, which leaves almost no time for anything else; any slow step in the loop means missed counts and a position error that builds up.[11]

Arduino's documentation names reading a rotary encoder as a good use for hardware interrupts: an interrupt lets the board catch every pulse while the main program gets on with other work.[11] When the chosen edge occurs on an interrupt-capable pin, the processor pauses the main program, runs a short Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) that updates the count, and then resumes. Variables shared with the main program must be declared volatile, and the ISR should be as short and fast as possible.[11] Some libraries go as far as writing the ISR in assembly language for speed.[12] The example below counts every change on Channel A (X2 decoding) and uses Channel B to decide the direction:

Widely used Arduino encoder libraries decode X4 with a 16-entry state table: the old and new states of A and B form a 4-bit index whose entry says whether the count changes by 0, +1, −1, or ±2 (when an edge was missed).[12][14] On larger processors the decoding is often done by a dedicated hardware quadrature counter rather than by software interrupts.[8] Some microcontrollers, such as the ESP32, include a hardware pulse-counter peripheral that can decode quadrature signals and filter glitches without running an ISR on every edge. Its counter is only 16 bits wide, so software must still extend the count and handle overflow.[15]

For robot arms and similar automation, US Digital recommends absolute encoders, because rotating a joint to find an index position "could be dangerous to the equipment or people in its environment".[1]

Six-axis industrial robot arms use absolute multi-turn encoders on their joints rather than incremental encoders because absolute encoders let the arm know its exact physical pose immediately on power-on, without dangerous homing movements through the cell.[1]

As an illustration, picture an industrial robot cell where an arm holds a heavy welding fixture inside a car body. With incremental encoders, an emergency stop or power outage would lose the joint positions, and to re-home the arm would have to move each joint until it found its home switch, possibly colliding with the car body and tooling on the way. With absolute encoders, the controller reads every joint angle as soon as power returns, with no movement, so production can resume safely.[1]

SSI (Synchronous Serial Interface): The encoder sends its position bits in step with a clock supplied by the controller, over two twisted pairs to the RS-422 standard, at clock rates up to 1.5 MHz depending on cable length. Communication is one-way, from encoder to controller.[6]

Electromagnetic Interference (EMI): Encoder signals are fast, low-voltage digital pulses. Running encoder wires alongside motor cables that carry PWM current can couple noise into them and cause false counts. Route encoder wiring away from motor power cables, and use twisted-pair or shielded cable where noise is a problem; industrial interfaces such as SSI use twisted pairs for this reason.[6] Industrial encoders reduce noise further with differential (RS-422 line-driver) outputs, which send each channel together with its inverse so that noise picked up equally on both wires cancels at the receiver.[18]

In real-world robotic systems, commanding actuators is never as simple as setting a fixed PWM duty cycle. If a mobile robot is commanded to drive forward at a constant 60% duty cycle, its speed will drop when it moves from smooth concrete to carpet, veer off-course if one wheel motor has slightly higher internal friction, and accelerate uncontrollably down an incline. Similarly, if an articulated robotic arm attempts to hold its joints at fixed motor voltages, gravity will pull the arm down toward the floor. Even the battery voltage sags under load, so the same command gives a different result as the robot works harder.[1] Feedback is how a controller copes with these disturbances.[2]

Rather than commanding raw actuator power, roboticists command a target setpoint (such as maintaining a velocity of 0.50 m/s or rotating an elbow joint to exactly 45.0 degrees). To reach and hold this target despite changing loads and disturbances, the robot must measure its actual state with feedback sensors (such as quadrature encoders), compute the tracking error and adjust its actuator commands automatically. The most widely used algorithm for this job is the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller: Åström and Murray state that more than 95% of all industrial control problems are solved by PID control, many of them with the derivative term left out (PI control).[2]

Specular Reflection and Absorption: The datasheet says the target should be a flat surface of not less than 0.5 m², as smooth as possible.[2] When a sound pulse strikes a smooth wall at a glancing angle, it can bounce away like light off a mirror (specular reflection) and never return to the receiver, so the robot may see the wall as an open corridor. Soft materials such as curtains or clothing absorb much of the sound and also return weak or no echoes.[1]

Laser Time-of-Flight (STMicroelectronics VL53L1X): A modern solid-state sensor that uses an invisible 940 nm Class 1 laser emitter (a Vertical-Cavity Surface-Emitting Laser, VCSEL) and a receiving array of Single-Photon Avalanche Diodes (SPADs).[6] Its main advantage over an infrared optical triangulation sensor is that it measures photon transit time, which makes its distance measurement largely independent of target color and surface reflectance.[6] The datasheet states it gives an absolute distance whatever the target colour and reflectance, although the maximum range still drops on dark targets (in the dark, about 360 cm on a white 88% target versus 170 cm on a grey 17% target in long mode). It measures up to 400 cm at up to 50 Hz over I2C, with a typical ranging error of about ±20 mm in the dark and a 27° field of view that can be narrowed to 15° by selecting a smaller region of interest. Strong ambient light shortens its range: with direct sunlight on the sensor, the long-mode range on a white target falls to about 73 cm.[6] In software, the VL53L1X trades range for robustness: short mode resists sunlight better, and a longer timing budget per reading improves accuracy at the cost of update rate.[7]

Infrared Reflectance Arrays (Pololu QTR-8RC): Pair an infrared emitter LED with an infrared phototransistor pointed directly downward toward the floor.[16] White surfaces reflect much more infrared light back to the phototransistor than dark matte tape, so the reading tells the robot whether it is over the line. The QTR-8RC places eight emitter and phototransistor pairs at a 9.525 mm (0.375 in) pitch. Pololu gives an optimal sensing distance of 3 mm (0.125 in) and a maximum recommended sensing distance of 9.5 mm (0.375 in); mounted higher than that, the contrast between line and floor becomes unreliable.[16]

Before an autonomous mobile robot can plan a collision-free path or drive to a target room, it must answer a basic question: Where am I? Outdoors, a GPS receiver can supply global coordinates, but GPS is a poor fit for indoor robots. The U.S. government's GPS site reports that GPS-enabled smartphones are typically accurate to within a 4.9 m radius under open sky, that accuracy worsens near buildings, bridges and trees, and that signal blockage and indoor or underground use are common causes of wrong positions.[1] An error of several meters is far too coarse for driving down a hallway.

The main weakness of dead reckoning is cumulative error growth. Each step updates the pose relative to the previous estimate, so any error made in one step is carried into every later position. With nothing outside the robot to pull the estimate back to the truth, the position error of odometry grows without bound.[2][5] ROS describes the same behavior: a robot's pose in the odom frame, which is built from odometry, can drift over time without any bounds, although it changes smoothly with no sudden jumps.[9] WPILib's documentation gives the same warning to student robot teams, adding that the drift is worse when the robot is bumped by other robots.[10]

To bring formal structure to robot behavior, engineers use a Finite State Machine (FSM).[2] An FSM is a mathematical model of computation made of a fixed set of states, incoming events and guarded transitions between states. At any instant, the robot is in exactly one state. By decoupling what the robot does (the state action) from when it switches behaviors (the state transition), state machines organize the "think" stage of the sense-think-act cycle into modular software components that are easier to check.
Transition: The deterministic move from the current (source) state to a target state, triggered when an event occurs and its associated guard evaluates to true.[2]

Action: Executable code invoked by the state machine. In classic automata theory, state machines execute actions either during states (a Moore machine) or during state transitions (a Mealy machine); Harel's statecharts allow both, and also allow actions on entering and on leaving a state.[2] In embedded robot code it is common to split a state's work into entry actions (executed once upon arrival, such as resetting a timer), execution actions (evaluated continuously each control loop), and exit actions (executed once upon departure, such as turning off an indicator LED).

This section is the lesson's own worked example. To observe an FSM in action, examine a differential-drive robot equipped with two analog floor reflectance sensors (A0 and A1), an HC-SR04 ultrasonic range finder (trigger pin 9, echo pin 10; the module measures roughly 2 cm to 4 m),[3] two DC motors controlled via PWM H-bridge drivers, and a normally high digital emergency stop push-button (pin 2).

Industrial machines use standardized state models too, so that machines from different vendors behave and report their status in the same way. ISA describes its machine-state technical report as a way to standardize "machine states, modes and PackTags" to improve interoperability.[9]

The international standard IEC 61131-3 defines the syntax and semantics of programming languages for Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs). The current edition (4.0, 2025) defines Structured Text, Ladder Diagram and Function Block Diagram, plus Sequential Function Chart (SFC) elements for structuring programs; the 2013 edition also included Instruction List.[10] PLCopen describes SFC as an additional set of graphical and textual elements, and the standard's SFC definitions are taken from the earlier function-chart standard IEC 848.[11] SFC models machine operations as a directed graph of:

Transitions: Boolean conditions between steps. A transition is enabled when all of its preceding steps are active, and it "clears" when it is enabled and its condition is true; clearing hands activity from the preceding steps to the following ones.[11]

Action Blocks and Qualifiers: The standard defines action qualifiers (ten in the PLCopen excerpt, including N, R, S, L, D and P).[11] As the CODESYS manual explains them: N (Non-stored) runs as long as the step is active; S (Set/Stored) keeps running after the step ends, until it is reset; R (Reset) stops a stored action; L (time Limited) runs until the step ends or a time span elapses; and D (time Delayed) starts only after the step has been active for a set delay.[12]

An ordinary ROS node starts working as soon as its process starts. If a motor controller node started before the laser scanner or safety supervisor was ready, the robot could move without its safety checks running. The ROS 2 design article on managed nodes gives the motivation for fixing this: a managed life cycle lets the launch system "ensure that all components have been instantiated correctly before it allows any component to begin executing its behaviour," and lets nodes be restarted or replaced while the system runs.[15]

Adding a new behavior can mean editing transitions in many existing states, which couples the code tightly. A related problem, which Harel called the "exponentially growing multitude of states," appears when independent behaviors are combined into one flat machine: two components with 1,000 states each give a product machine with a million states.[2]

The package documentation describes how to split estimation between two filter instances. An instance that also fuses global absolute data such as GPS uses the map frame, and something else (normally the first instance) must provide the odom → base_link transform. The most widely taught profile is the trapezoidal velocity profile. Picture a rest-to-rest move of distance D. The axis accelerates at a constant rate amax until it reaches the speed limit vmax, cruises at vmax, and then decelerates at amax until it stops exactly at the target. Plotted against time, the velocity rises in a straight ramp, stays flat, and falls in a straight ramp: a trapezoid. One survey describes this profile, with its constant-acceleration, constant-velocity and constant-deceleration phases, as the most common one for industrial robot trajectory planning.[3]

The field of view is the physical inspection area that must fill the camera sensor, while working distance is the physical clearance between the front of the lens and the inspected object. In the factory, machine vision begins with illumination.

A machine vision camera cannot inspect features it cannot see. Desired image quality can typically be achieved by improving system illumination rather than investing in higher resolution detectors or lenses.[1] For example, an expensive high-resolution camera paired with a precision lens will still produce unusable results if improper lighting creates harsh glare or deep shadows. In contrast, an inexpensive sensor placed under an optimized lighting geometry yields clean, consistent images that simple, fast algorithms can process reliably.

Industrial inspection tasks broadly fall into four categories: dimensional gauging, presence verification, surface flaw detection, and code reading. Every visual measurement begins with optical sampling. When an engineer selects a camera and lens for a gauging station, they must determine whether the system can physically resolve the smallest required tolerance. A simple measure of sensor resolution is the number of pixels per millimeter.[2] For example, if a camera sensor has 2,400 pixels along its horizontal axis and images an inspection field of view that is 120 mm wide, the optical system delivers exactly 20 pixels per millimeter in object space.

However, sensor pixel count alone does not guarantee that fine edges or small defects can be resolved clearly. As 7.1 explained, optical resolution is measured in line pairs per millimeter and the Nyquist limit is two pixels per line pair,[3] and the lens must also keep enough contrast between the bars.[4] For gauging, this means that if the physical detail in object space is smaller than two sensor pixels, the vision system cannot reliably detect it or establish its boundary location.

Every image message begins with a standard ROS header structure containing timing and coordinate frame metadata. In sensor_msgs/Image the header timestamp represents image acquisition time and frame_id specifies the optical frame of the camera.[2] A driver should stamp each image with the time it was captured, which is needed to synchronize vision data with joint encoder states when a robot arm moves during eye-in-hand image acquisition or when tracking moving conveyor belts.

The frame_id field ties the camera data to the robot kinematic coordinate tree maintained by the TF2 transform library. In the ROS optical camera coordinate frame, +x points right, +y points down, and +z points into the image plane.[2] This optical convention places the coordinate origin directly at the camera's optical center. This differs from standard robot body coordinate frames (where +x points forward, +y points left, and +z points upward), which is why transform trees are needed when mapping 2D pixel coordinates into 3D robot grasping poses.

The CameraInfo message specifies mathematical models of lens distortion and projective geometry. The plumb_bob distortion model in sensor_msgs/CameraInfo represents standard radial and tangential lens distortion.[3] The distortion parameters array D for the plumb_bob model consists of five coefficients: k1, k2, t1, t2, and k3.[3] Coefficients k1, k2, k3 model radial lens distortion (such as barrel or pincushion distortion), while coefficients t1, t2 model tangential distortion caused by slight physical misalignments between optical glass elements and the sensor plane.

Explicit messages in EtherNet/IP use TCP for request-reply client-server transactions addressed to the Message Router object.[2] Unlike cyclic I/O, explicit messages are acyclic: they are sent only as needed. Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) gives explicit messages reliable delivery over point-to-point connections, with error checking and retries. Integrators use explicit messaging for tasks that do not need deterministic delivery every cycle, such as reading fault logs, reconfiguring drive parameters, or querying firmware versions.

Applications on industrial networks must recognize and handle rejected requests. When a Modbus server cannot carry out a request, its exception response uses the request function code plus 0x80.[4] For example, if a client submits a read holding registers request using function code 0x03, an exception response carries function code 0x83 (calculated as 0x03 + 0x80 = 131 in decimal notation).

While the black channel concept allows safety data to ride on standard cables, it places strict requirements on physical device design. Implementing the PROFIsafe protocol cannot turn a standard device into a safety device without safety hardware architecture.[2] The final safety level of a device is set by the architecture of its safety hardware.[2] The device also does not have to reach the protocol's maximum level: PROFIsafe is suitable up to SIL 3, but an F-device only needs the level its safety function requires.[2] For drives, IEC 61800-5-2 defines safety stopping and monitoring functions for drives with integrated safety, called F-drives.[2]

Every MQTT application message has a Topic Name and a Quality of Service.[4] Clients publish messages to the server (often called a broker) under a topic name such as plant/cell_2/robot_1/temperature, and the server forwards them to the clients that subscribed to that topic, so publishers and subscribers never connect to each other directly.

For example, an automated guided vehicle (AGV) transporting parts between cells publishes its battery voltage to topic agv_3/battery every ten seconds with QoS 0, while publishing batch completion notices to topic agv_3/completed on port 8883 with QoS 2 to ensure the inventory database records the delivery without duplication.
